title: Session Drain
notes: Close every open swarm session so substrate surgery begins with zero in-flight work. Nothing else in the rebuild is safe while a worker is mid-lifecycle on the very substrate being replaced.

title: Bounded MCP Reads
notes: Bring every MCP list read under Lambda's 6 MB synchronous response ceiling by moving heavy blob columns out to by-id reads. A list read that grows past the ceiling fails outright rather than degrading, so the bound has to be structural rather than a habit of asking for less.

title: Dual-Path Purge
notes: Eliminate dual-path git access — the corruption class where one repository is reachable by two different paths and two writers disagree about which one is real. Symlinks deleted, repos moved out of Desktop into real directories, every git call audited, PR finalisation made read-only, Primary sync forced fast-forward-only, and a hard clean-tree gate on the Primary.

title: Wontfix Fold-In
notes: Disposition the wontfix backlog, folding the still-live scope into the substrate work that supersedes it rather than carrying dead rows forward into the rebuild.

title: Substrate Validation
notes: Prove the repaired substrate by running a complete worker lifecycle end to end on it. The first clean run also surfaced and fixed the statusline dev-server indicator.

title: Test Repair
notes: Repair every pre-existing test failure — backend fixture drift, MCP count assertions, two harness scripts — so the suite reads truly green. A suite carrying known failures cannot serve as a regression baseline, because nobody can tell a new break from an old one.

title: Green Baseline
notes: Record the all-passing regression baseline across every suite: the fixed reference point the clone-substrate cutover is measured against. Recorded 2026-07-26 — harness 3736/3736, Lambda-Rest 134, Cognito 18, MCP unit 252, integration 688, production 62, all passing.

title: WSL MCP Setup
notes: Stand up the MCP daemon on the Windows/WSL machine: bring its workspace current, migrate credentials, then start the daemon. Strictly serial in that order. Runnable whenever the user is physically at that machine, which is the only real constraint on it.

title: WSL MCP Validation
notes: First of three Windows/WSL verifications: full MCP validation — health, wrapper read and mutation round-trips, bounded list reads, all three daemon test tiers, and auto-restart.

title: Mirror Layer + Clone Substrate Core
notes:
The mirror layer and its protections, landed as a reviewable unit before any cutover work depends on them: a single-writer mirror updater with a mandatory synchronous fetch at every provision, a per-repo lock and loud failure, plus fully-private clones with no hardlinks. Greenfield-verified.

--- merged from step 'Clone Substrate Core' (req #3485, 2026-08-12): both steps carried requirement #3077 alone, and Pipeline 2.0 seats a requirement on exactly one step. Merged rather than dropping a seat, so no permanently-pending gate is imported into the 2.0 copy of this completed plan. ---

The clone substrate itself — discovery and provisioning cutover behind a flag, dual-mode cleanup, and the worker git guard that refuses any mutation aimed outside its own session. Wrapped in feature review, gap analysis and a full regression against the recorded baseline.

title: Agent Context Polish
notes: Polish pass on the Agent Context work, run from the Windows/WSL machine. Corrected 2026-07-26: the session was created after the credential migration completed, so it ran on the new daemon from birth — no stale-stack risk, and the normal lifecycle applies.

title: Gate Remediation
notes: Remediate what the substrate gate reviews found: no-hardlink cloning (the tests asserted the opposite), freshness-window dedup with a stale-ok degrade path, the skill cutover away from hardcoded worktree paths that would have broken at flip time, an attribution coverage fix, and tests for the medium and low findings. This is the work that has to land before the flag can flip or the canaries can run.

title: Gate Reviews + Flip
notes: Primary-run gate execution: the feature review and the gap review, an independent regression pass after remediation, then flipping the default provisioning mode to clone. The reviews found 5 deviations and 12 gaps. Mirrors and sessions layout created and 7 mirrors seeded 2026-07-26.

title: Clone Canary 1
notes: First live canary: a docs-only requirement runs a clone-provisioned session through its entire lifecycle. The work is deliberately trivial — the substrate is what is under test, not the change.

title: WSL Clone Testing
notes: Second of three Windows/WSL verifications: repeat the canaries on that machine — mirrors and session-clone layout through the same scripts, a real full lifecycle, write isolation, machine-pin routing. The clone mechanism is proven per machine and never assumed portable.

title: Clone Canary 2
notes: Second canary, exercising everything the first could not: two or more repos, a mid-session checkout of a third, an npm install inside the session clone, dev-server registration, a pause-resume-undo round trip, the deploy path, and the mid-flight recursive-delete isolation test.

title: Trust Dialog Fix
notes: Major canary catch: clone sessions are new project roots, so Claude Code's folder-trust dialog silently blocked both canaries — worktrees had been inheriting trust through their .git pointer, which nobody had noticed because nothing else ever created a new root. Fixed same-day by pre-registering the trust entry before backend dispatch.

title: Backlog Wave
notes: Seven parallel sessions on the now-proven substrate — the first real test that it carries concurrent load, and a backlog drain in its own right: house dialog pattern, integrity-error to 409 mapping, junction POST 500 fix, editable Documents page, agent telemetry collection, delete-dialog wording test, and the sort-order invariant decision.

title: Post-Wave Batch
notes: Five sessions in one launch, cleaning up what the parallel wave exposed: a Python-version fix in venv provisioning, per-repo provisioning telemetry persisted to the session record, a cross-session write from the stale-daemon restarter into the Primary clone, E2E coverage for the editable instruction registry, and a cross-tenant read-back leak on profile creation.

title: Instructions Table View
notes: Harden the generic edit-in-place table pattern by applying it to the instructions registry — the pattern's second real consumer, which is what turns it from a one-off into a pattern.

title: Primary Relocation
notes: Plan-completion gate. Relocate the Primary AI to the workspace root through the same clone pattern workers use, migrate memory, config and the MCP daemon, and decommission the old path with no dual-path overlap. The validation battery ends with a canary swarm launch from the new home, because nothing short of that proves the move.

title: Orchestration Spec
notes:
The discuss session that specced pipelines-as-data and filed the feature's follow-on requirements. This plan is its own seed dataset, which is what made the design concrete rather than theoretical. Batched with the change that makes swarm closeout take its RDS snapshot without asking: a protection with exactly one right answer should never have been a permission prompt.

This plan's own tracking requirement is deliberately not linked here. It is a container rather than work, so it stays open for the life of the plan and would pin this step Running forever.

title: Agentic Telemetry Batch
notes: Two sessions in one launch on agent telemetry: per-document actual-token capture for architecture documents, and machine, model and effort columns on telemetry runs.

title: Token Ground-Truth
notes: Establish a ground-truth breakdown of Claude Code's base token figure, rather than continuing to reason from an estimate. User-driven, on the Windows/WSL machine.

title: Foundation Wave
notes: The foundation of pipelines-as-data, three sessions in one launch: grooming the design intent into the architect documents, the schema — epic, feature and requirement hierarchy plus the pipeline tables, API routes and dev fixtures seeded from this plan — and the ordering and derivation engine with self-checking invariants.

title: API + Table Wave
notes: The MCP API over the new schema — bounded resources and echo-verified mutation tools with a single-read plan render — and the first UI on top of it, a plan-rows table per pipeline. The single-read render is the load-bearing part: a per-step fan-out would make plan size the cost driver.

title: Visualizer + Doctrine Wave
notes: Three strands that together make the feature usable: the plan visualizer with drag-pan, three-level zoom and clickable steps; the Primary's execution doctrine with its mutation playbook and fail-loud watchdog; and the server-side cost rollup. Batched with the junction authorization fix the schema work flagged — an unscoped junction read was returning every user's rows.

title: Acceptance Battery
notes: Acceptance: end-to-end tests over the seeded plan, plus a replay of all eight recorded mutation classes through the MCP tools, asserting derived state and invariant-clean order after each one. Replaying the mutation classes is what proves derivation holds under editing, not just on a static fixture.

title: Polish + Showcase
notes: Final polish and showcase — the feature's only user-review stop. Re-seed the dev database with the full live plan, run a cosmetic pass, deep-link the dev server to the plan view, and walk the user through it.

title: Messaging Design
notes: Design discussion for a cooperative inter-Claude message system, grounded by the shipped orchestration core and the Primary doctrine. Explores how a Primary and its workers might communicate proactively rather than only by leaving rows in a database for each other to find.

title: Migration Numbering
notes: Migration numbers collide when concurrent sessions each pick the next integer by hand — three sessions independently chose the same one. Decide a collision-proof scheme, normalise the existing collisions safely, and enforce uniqueness with a test so the scheme cannot quietly lapse.

title: Primary Cutover
notes: Execute the Primary relocation: a fresh user session runs the cutover runbook, moving the Primary to the workspace root and retiring the legacy root. Deliberately not a swarm session — the old-home Primary hands off and retires, which it cannot do from inside itself. Hard precondition: no swarm session in flight.

title: WSL Primary Parity
notes: Third of three Windows/WSL verifications: full primary-session independence on that machine — run the cutover runbook there, decommission the old path, and run the validation battery from the new home.

title: Relocation Verification
notes: Human-verified acceptance battery for the relocation, executed by the new Primary session from its new home: layout resolution, MCP, statusline walk-ups, dev server, a canary launch, hooks and config, and an old-path decommission audit. Failures file defects rather than being patched inline — a verification pass that repairs what it finds has stopped being a verification pass.

title: FK Grief-Lock Fix
notes: Close the cross-tenant foreign-key grief-lock: ownership-check the target of every reference on a creator-scoped table. The attack does not defeat row scoping, it rides on it — an attacker writes a row of their own, which passes every existing check, that merely points at a victim's parent. On a restrict-delete column the victim can then never delete that parent again, blocked by a row they cannot see, list or remove, with no self-service recovery. It waits only because the deployment is effectively single-tenant today, which is a property of how Darwin is run rather than of the code.

title: Data-Layer Decisions
notes: Two discuss sessions in one launch on data-layer policy: whether dev-database schema tests can be isolated from concurrent session DDL, and whether to enable strict SQL mode. Both are decisions with real trade-offs rather than defects with one right answer, which is why they get a conversation instead of an implementation.

title: Closeout Gate
notes: Enforcement for the partial-closeout breach: a session may no longer complete while leaving its requirement non-terminal, unless a follow-on requirement is filed and the closeout is scoped to what was actually delivered. Adds the deployed-worker doctrine and the multi-executor authoring split rule, with harness tests. The breach that prompted it merged, deployed and destroyed its own session while abandoning its requirement — nothing detected it, and the session was gone before anyone could look.

title: Combined ride map
notes: The aggregator card's first half: render the concatenated GPS tracks of every selected ride on one map, the way the export map already does for a single ride.

title: Photo aggregation
notes: The aggregator card's second half: discover the photos falling inside each selected ride's time window and place them as markers on the same combined map, so a season of riding reads as one picture.

title: Meta-pattern doc
notes: Write the aggregator meta-pattern up as a document, with its two canonical implementations side by side: the requirements aggregator and the mapping one. Two instances is what makes it a pattern rather than a coincidence, and writing it down is what stops the third from being improvised.

title: Planning pattern
notes: Capture the epic planning pattern as a binding instruction — how an epic is decomposed into features and executable steps — so it is repeatable rather than re-derived from scratch each time.

title: Validation Phase
notes: Prove the aggregator feature actually works, and close what the build left thin. The gap analysis decides which untested paths genuinely matter rather than chasing coverage for its own sake; the map-coordinate read path pays down its performance and documentation debt; the card gets component-level tests. This is where defects are meant to be found, because the polish-and-demo pass that follows is judged by the user's own eye rather than by a green suite, and anything still broken surfaces there in front of them.

title: Capstone demo
notes: Capstone: a polish pass over everything the plan built, then a demo. Victory is gated on the user's own review rather than on a green suite, because the thing being judged is whether it is nice to use.

title: Lesson Learned
notes: First of the agentic refactor: three instruction requirements authored in one launch — the executive-summary instruction, the polish pattern, and the reflection pattern. User-driven content, because an instruction that Claude wrote for itself is not guidance, it is a mirror.

title: Guiding Principles and Data Refactor
notes: Second of the agentic refactor: restructure the instruction registry around guiding principles, and refactor the data behind it, so that an instruction has a stated reason rather than only a rule.

title: Agentic Cleanup
notes: Third of the agentic refactor: author the two missing guiding-principles charters, AWS Architect and Agents Architect. The relationship they occupy only exists once the registry refactor has landed, which is why they were not written alongside the others.

title: Dev-server machine scoping
notes: Correct the dev-server delete path so a registration is resolved and removed against the machine that actually owns it.

title: Swarm-Start Eligibility
notes:
Stop offering a launch that is not the caller's to make.

A requirement carried by a plan step is not eligible for a direct swarm-start - its launch belongs to the coordinator, at the point the plan says so. Every surface that offers a requirement for launch must therefore show only the ones no step has claimed.

The two populations are told apart today by requirement status, maintained by hand - a second, hand-copied version of a fact the database already holds exactly in the step-requirement junction. Hand-copied facts drift, and this one did: three pipelined requirements sat in the wrong status while the rest sat in another, and eight more were briefly moved during a recovery. Deriving it removes the copy rather than tidying it.

Scope is deliberately wider than the aggregator card that prompted it: every skill and script that selects, offers, lists or launches a requirement gets the same filter, and the report names every surface examined including those needing no change. Fixing the card and leaving a skill behind would leave the defect exactly where it is hardest to notice.

Also absorbed here is a user-facing filter for the requirements browse page, migrated from a duplicate requirement. That case is different from the launch surfaces and is treated differently: on a page that merely lists work, both populations are legitimate to look at, so it gets a toggle rather than a silent exclusion. Its valuable state is ON - the residue it reveals is work nobody has scheduled, findable today only by reading a plan and a requirement list side by side.

Moved into this epic 2026-08-01 at the user's direction: the work is plan-eligibility work, and it was previously seated with the parallel fix wave only because that is where it was first noticed.

title: Primary closeout on clone substrate
notes: The Primary closeout path is broken on the clone substrate. Worth going first when capacity is limited, because until it lands no product-repo change can be closed out by the Primary at all.

title: Primary-sync hook removal
notes: Remove the automatic primary-sync hooks. An automatic sync that fires on someone else's schedule is exactly the kind of unrequested write the substrate rebuild spent its life eliminating. Touches the config repo, plus a machine-local statusline follow-up.

title: dateFormat UTC normalization
notes: Timestamps in the T-form are parsed as local time, so a date renders a day off depending on the viewer's timezone. Touches the Darwin repo only, and retires the workaround the pipeline view model currently carries for it — the workaround being the evidence that the bug is real and already load-bearing.

title: Vite Topology rung retirement
notes: Retire the hardcoded developer-machine path rung from the Vite config, and un-skip the mirror test that has been asserting around it. A skipped test guarding a hardcoded path is two problems pretending to be none.

title: Tracking-Req Exemption
notes:
A plan's own tracking requirement is a container, not work — it stays open for the plan's whole life, so without an exemption it pins its step Running forever. Make that signal a durable column rather than a per-session judgement call.

The exemption has to land in the UI's derivation before a second engine duplicates the same predicate, or the two disagree about the same step from day one.

The requirement itself was approved with no feature and no linked step — invisible to every plan-shaped read, and it would simply never have been sequenced. That it had to be found by hand is the argument for the sync report.

title: Pipeline Agent
notes: Give the orchestration feature a named owner in the agent registry, with custody of its documents. Deliberately not treated as a prerequisite for the engine: the engine's design is already settled by the specification session, so serializing code behind a documentation groom would buy nothing.

title: Pipeline Engine
notes:
One durable engine replacing the per-gate watch-and-re-arm trigger model, so that a plan mutation becomes simply the next cycle's input instead of a reason to tear down and rebuild the watch.

The finding that made it possible: the doctrine's premise that the Primary is re-invoked only when a process exits is false. Measured — a monitored process delivered five stdout lines about twenty seconds apart while still running.

title: Orchestrator Skills
notes:
The two skills that drive the engine: one that loads the plan, reports what has drifted, dry-runs the real cycle, gates on approval and then orchestrates; and one that ends the orchestrator without touching the work it launched. Start and stop only — no pause, unpause, undo or restart, per user directive.

The first three phases write nothing, which is what makes the whole approach abortable right up to the gate.

title: Session-Pipeline Link
notes:
A durable record of which plan and which epic a swarm session was advancing. Left until late deliberately: the engine and the skills are what define what the linkage is for, so specifying it earlier would have been guessing.

Stamped once and never overwritten, because the fact is history. Every link a derivation would walk is mutable, so a derived answer would rewrite a finished session's attribution the moment the plan was edited.

title: Pipeline Resync
notes:
Re-attach a Primary AI to an in-flight orchestration after its context is cleared. The engine is a process and keeps running; a resync skill works out what it was orchestrating and rejoins.

An expected token-saving pattern rather than error recovery — it exists so that clearing mid-run is a supported move instead of a mistake. It reads only, and deliberately never restarts a dead engine, because that would re-establish a standing launch grant nobody re-approved.

title: Condensation Grouping Fix
notes:
Two measured defects in the shared grouping key behind launch batching and condensation proposals.

It has no epic term, so it proposed merging mapping steps with swarm-backlog steps into a single step — and a merged row derives one dominant epic, which would hand one epic's requirements to the other epic's Primary.

It also keys on the raw dependency set rather than the remaining unsatisfied gate, so steps with identical empty gates get three different keys. That second defect has zero blast radius today only because the first one accidentally separates those same steps anyway.

title: Haiku Swarm-Command Gate
notes:
Gate swarm skill invocations when the session running them is on Haiku, with a per-invocation override.

The gate is on the model running the skill, not the model the work uses — swarm may still freely operate on sessions and requirements that use Haiku. The mechanism that resolves the running model is undetermined, and is the substance of the work rather than a detail of it.

Not provably file-disjoint from the primary-sync hook removal: if the chosen mechanism turns out to be a hook, both edit the same settings file. Verify before running them concurrently.

title: Regression Re-assessment
notes:
The orchestration loop must treat a requirement moving backward as a first-class event. Verified absent from the whole second-generation specification.

Live case: a session was undone about an hour in, its requirement returned to launch-ready, and the step was immediately re-launchable. A human noticed. Nothing in the engine as specified would have.

The design tension IS the requirement: the engine must not re-launch a step it just launched, but must re-launch one that regressed — and a local launched-set satisfies the first while being structurally incapable of the second. Resolution: hold no launched-set at all. Launching moves the requirement forward, so the next derivation suppresses it automatically, and the only bookkeeping needed is a short debounce covering the window between emitting a launch and the session recording itself. That debounce must expire rather than latch.

Regression out of a terminal status is a different event and gets different handling: dependents may already have launched on that completion, so it is reported loudly and never auto-launched.

Also in scope, same root: a step deriving Running with no live session behind it is a silent stall, and must be reported rather than waited on.

title: Path-Audit Fixture Exemption
notes:
The path audit's workspace-path assertion fails on a clean tree, because the conformance corpus embeds requirement prose that happens to quote the path. Those are fixture data, not live references, and the corpus has to stay a faithful snapshot to be worth anything.

That assertion is the precondition gating the Windows/WSL cutover. A standing false positive trains people to ignore the one check that must not be ignored on the day it matters.

title: Engine Emits Late-Linked Requirements
notes:
The engine fires a launch line only on an eligibility edge, so a requirement linked to a step that was already eligible and already commanded is never emitted — nobody launches it, and nothing says so.

Must not run concurrently with the regression re-assessment work: both change the same emission logic and the same edge-detection state, in a module that was only just created. Kept as separate work rather than merged because they are separately filed and separately verifiable; the shared root is that edge detection is too coarse, and whichever lands second should confirm the first's trigger still fires.

title: SQL Database-Target Safety
notes:
Every SQL file carries a USE statement naming production, which overrides the connection's default database — so a caller aimed at the dev database silently writes production instead.

Demonstrated 2026-08-01: a code-review probe believed to be targeting a scratch database wrote three production rows. They were removed and production independently re-verified through the gateway.

Also in scope: the dev-database recreate script needs a confirmation gate, having emptied the dev database in the same incident; the dev database's areas and tasks need a decided state; and a known build-visualizer table gap must be recorded as permanently intended rather than rediscovered annually.

Second-order question to resolve: if every migration carries that statement, then the documented apply-to-dev-first gate cannot be satisfied by running the file at all. Establish whether the workflow has been hand-editing that line each time — if so, the documentation is part of the defect.

title: Pipeline Backlog
notes:
One launch unit for the accumulated pipeline backlog: the missing delete tool, plan-fixture cost coverage, seed-documentation count drift, the status-line orchestration display, derivation-parity polish, sibling-repo resolution on the clone substrate, and visualizer polish.

Consolidated 2026-08-01 from seven separate rows. Each had been ungated, which rendered them at the far left of the plan - visually claiming they run first, ahead of the work they actually follow - and seven rows where one will do. Design rule 2 supports the shape: requirements sharing a gate and run mode belong in one step, not seven.

For a while this step also carried a deliberately arbitrary edge whose only purpose was to push it rightwards in the layout. That workaround was retired once the axis began reading as time, which is exactly the outcome the layout work existed to produce.

Note that the machine pins are not uniform across the seven, so automatic batching would not have grouped these on its own. This is a deliberate authoring choice rather than a derived batch.

title: Time-Axis Plan Layout
notes:
Make the plan visualizer's horizontal axis read as time rather than dependency depth, and stack epic bands by derived start rather than by first appearance.

Verified mechanism: a dependency-less step got depth zero, depth became the column, and bands stacked in the order they first appeared. So a brand-new epic, having no edges yet, landed in the far-left column claiming it ran first.

The evidence was in this plan itself. The backlog step carried a deliberately arbitrary edge whose only purpose was to push it rightwards. A layout correctable only by lying in the data is the defect, and removing that workaround was in scope - it has since been retired.

Hard constraint: horizontal position is a topological invariant - a step always renders to the right of its dependencies, which is what makes the arcs readable - and topology outranks presentation. Time must be an origin offset or a tie-break within a band, never a replacement for depth. Cross-epic edges are live in this plan, so an arc forced backwards across a band boundary is a real case to design for, not a hypothetical.

title: Launch Line-Buffer Clear
notes:
Prefix the injected worker-launch command with a line clear, so keystrokes typed while the terminal window is still appearing cannot join the command.

Verified why this works: the launcher injects the whole launch as one write, and the auto-prompt is a shell command argument rather than typing into Claude Code's interface. So stray keystrokes land in the shell's line buffer, where clearing them costs nothing. In a running interface the same trick would submit the junk as a prompt — here Claude has not started yet, so it cannot.

The failure today: the user types a few characters as the window appears, the injected text appends to them, and the session never starts. The window sits at a shell prompt looking launched.

A newline is probably the wrong primitive, because it clears the buffer by executing it. Kill-line clears without executing and is strictly safer. Verify the control character survives the launcher's escaping rather than assuming it does.

Scope limit: this covers keystrokes before the injection only. Anything typed after Claude starts goes to the interface, and no launch-command prefix can help. The same exposure exists in the Windows/WSL launcher — fix both, or state why not.

title: Epic View Centering
notes:
Clicking an epic name zooms and pans that epic's requirements to fill the viewport, with margin on all four sides.

Composition, not new machinery — verified 2026-08-01: the visualizer already runs d3-zoom over the canvas with a zoom ref, a transform state and a fit-to-width base scale, and the layout already computes every band's vertical extent, with horizontal extent derivable from the band's own steps. The fit rectangle is therefore already computable; the work is turning it into a transform.

Not a mode, per user correction: the click sets the viewport once and then it is as if the code never ran. No focus state, no selected epic, no toggle, no reset, no restore-previous-view. The user pans, zooms and clicks afterwards exactly as before. An implementation that stores a focused-epic flag and branches on it later has misread this.

The likely bug is the same point: apply the transform through the zoom behavior, never by setting React state directly. The behavior holds its own transform, so writing state alone makes the next wheel or drag snap back to the stale value. Going through the behavior is also exactly what makes as-if-it-never-ran literally true, because its transform simply becomes the new current one.

Four things to decide: the screen-space padding constant; a maximum-zoom ceiling that respects the existing scale extent, since a one-step epic would otherwise zoom absurdly; making the band header both hit-testable and visibly clickable; and which level-of-detail the fit lands on, since text draws in world coordinates.

Coordinate with the time-axis work, which changes band order and adds per-band horizontal origins — nothing here may assume bands are in first-appearance order. This also shares the visualizer component with the polish work in the backlog, and two sessions in that component at once is a real conflict.

title: Plan Visualizer Time Ruler
notes:
Draw the time ruler. The plan visualizer's horizontal axis became a calendar - columns are time slots, one per distinct day carrying work plus a trailing future slot, ordered chronologically with dependency depth as a hard floor so every arc still points forward. Nothing renders it. The layout exports the slot list and a step-to-slot map; the canvas consumes neither, so the columns are ordered by time but a reader cannot read them as dates.

The shape is open by design: a date strip along the top, subtle separators at slot origins, a tinted future region, or some combination.

The zero-overlap contract is the acceptance gate. The layout tests assert that no two label rectangles intersect and no label intersects a bead, across all four layout combinations. A ruler consuming vertical space shifts every band, so its rectangles belong in the same label set the existing invariant already covers - not in a second, untested class of text.

Zoom is a pure transform and a level change must never relayout, so any reserved ruler height is unconditional.

Slots are dense in columns but can be sparse in time - two adjacent columns may be days apart. Decide whether the ruler says so. Labels must degrade on a long plan (every Nth day, or month boundaries) rather than overlap.

Held behind the visualizer work already in flight: the slot model it reads must exist first, and three other requirements are editing the same component and layout module. Concurrent sessions in that file is the merge conflict the swarm rules exist to avoid - and is precisely why this was split out rather than folded into the axis change.

title: Navbar Session Expansion
notes:
Sessions in the navigation sidebar gain a third level: a session expands to reveal its starts, completes and undos, collapsible like every other level.

The sublevel is a coherent set rather than an arbitrary grouping - a session's birth record, its closeout, and any abandonment are the three things that ever happened to it, so expanding a session is really asking what became of it.

Three presentation options, and the choice is the user's rather than the implementer's: an expand icon recoloured to the Darwin scheme that reveals the sublevel on click; a count after each entry showing how many third-level items it holds; or a plus/minus indicator in place of that count. Offer all three and let the user pick - the requirement deliberately does not choose.

title: Orchestration Doctrine And Rules
notes:
Write down the rules the plan actually runs by - four groomings that all land in the same documents.

They are one step because they are one file set and one author's job. The orchestrate verb needs codifying as its eight rules; the definition of a BATCH needs to exist somewhere quotable, since it is what two design rules produce and it is currently written only in a function docstring; the orchestrator's judgement lessons need a home, because the doctrine covers the mechanics of orchestrating and says almost nothing about the decisions; and descriptions need a rule against duplicating what the database already holds, with the sync report reconciled to it and a mechanical check so it is not a convention.

The four interlock rather than merely coexist. The batch definition is required BY the orchestrate instruction, whose rules for absorbing into a launch unit and for launching a batch command both turn on what a launch unit is and currently assume it. Two of the judgement lessons amend that same instruction - one adds a narrow autonomy exception, the other sharpens what a dependency edge is allowed to mean. And the description rule and the batch definition both land in the design-rules document alongside the ten. Four sessions here would be four editors of the same paragraphs.

The description rule carries the only substantial code in the step, and it is not optional: the sync report's prose-diff categories were built to compare a hand-written id list against the rows, and once the prose stops carrying ids one category reports everything and two report nothing. Measured after the live plan was remediated, one category went from nine findings to thirty-five. A category that can only ever report everything, or only ever nothing, must be removed or re-pointed deliberately.

title: Canvas: L1 Label Gate
notes:
Stop drawing the step name at the outermost zoom level - a gate that existed and was removed by the visualizer polish pass.

First of four sequential passes over the plan canvas, and deliberately the smallest. It goes first because it ESTABLISHES the level condition the next pass has to respect: the pop-up work gives that same label a hit region, and a hit target over text that is no longer drawn is an invisible hotspot handing the user a card from empty space. Doing the gate first means the second session inherits a condition to match rather than a bug to discover.

The gate hides the DRAW and never the layout. The label's rectangle stays in the geometry at every level, or zoom stops being a pure transform and the zero-overlap invariant becomes level-dependent.

The four canvas requirements were originally seated as one step, which would have launched four concurrent sessions into one component - two of them editing the same three lines. A step is a launch unit of REQUIREMENTS, and each requirement gets its own session; one step does not mean one author. Split into a chain 2026-08-01 before launch.

title: Epic Editor Page
notes:
The first of three sibling editor pages: a formal epic editor as a second-level navigation entry under Pipelines, wiring through to the editing surface that already exists for an epic.

It goes first and alone deliberately. All three pages add an entry to the same navigation tree and a route to the same route table, so three concurrent sessions would collide in two shared files - and the first page is where the pattern gets decided. The two that follow copy a shipped page rather than inventing a parallel dialect of it, which is the actual reason for sequencing rather than a merge-conflict technicality.

Held behind the navigation work that added a third level beneath sessions, for the same reason: one writer at a time in that component.

title: Epic Label: Palette
notes:
Make the epic band colours survive a dark background - brown and its muddy neighbours out, every colour clearly separated from the panel, and a build-failing check so dirt cannot drift back in.

First of three sequential passes over the epic band label, and deliberately first because it is the only one that changes NO GEOMETRY. A colour change alters nothing about label width, so the two passes that follow do not have to be re-checked against it - whereas either of them landing first would force this one to re-verify collisions it had nothing to do with.

The guard is the substance rather than the hex values. Brown is not a hue - it is dark, desaturated orange - so a hue blocklist will not catch it. The check is two-dimensional: minimum contrast against the actual panel colour, minimum saturation, and a higher floor for warm hues where dirt lives. Thresholds get measured against the colours being kept and removed, and recorded with a reason, because a threshold nobody can justify is relaxed the first time it is inconvenient.

The three label requirements were originally one step, which would have launched three concurrent sessions into one rectangle. A step is a launch unit of REQUIREMENTS and each gets its own session; one step does not mean one author. Split into a chain 2026-08-01 before launch.

title: Engine Output Path Isolation
notes:
A second orchestrator launch destroys the first one's edge stream, and the failure is silent on both sides.

The engine writes to a fixed path keyed only by scope. A second launch on a scope already being orchestrated truncates that file with its redirect BEFORE the scope guard refuses it - so the refusal works exactly as designed while the damage is already done. The first engine, alive and healthy, keeps writing at its old offset into a now-truncated file; the file goes sparse and the first window's monitor sees nothing more.

Both halves are quiet. The second window is told it was refused, which reads as no harm done. The first window simply stops receiving edges from a process it can still see running - which is indistinguishable from a plan with nothing happening in it.

Found in code review rather than in use, which is worth noting: an orchestration that lost its edges would most likely have been read as a stalled plan.

title: Sibling Repo Test Gate
notes:
Cross-repo security-invariant tests hard-fail on a clone session instead of resolving or skipping honestly.

A companion requirement already fixed cross-repo FILE resolution for the unit tier: read from this session's own checkout, else from the verified workspace mirror, and refuse anything that cannot be vouched for with a message naming the command that fixes it. The full-validation tier was not converted and still resolves a DIRECTORY, failing outright when the sibling repo is absent.

What that takes down matters more than the inconvenience: these are the tests asserting that every creator-scoped table is registered for authorization. A table missing from that registry means the gateway accepts unscoped reads and writes against it - and one genuinely was missing before an audit caught it. A test that cannot run on the default session substrate is not protecting anything.

Convert it to the same resolve-or-refuse contract, so an absent sibling produces a named, actionable skip rather than a red suite everyone learns to ignore.

title: Worker Orchestration Indicator
notes:
Give a swarm worker the orchestration indicator the Primary already has, and find out whether a worker can genuinely orchestrate at all.

This sat unbuildable for a long time because it was split out of its parent with a two-word body - Deliverable #2 said only Session Status Line - and guessing at it was refused rather than fabricated. The spec is now given, so what remains is ordinary work.

The display half is nearly free and was never the hard part. The gate is a single emptiness test on the requirement id, which is what makes the segment Primary-only; the marker, the scope registry, the run record and the resolver already exist and already work. What must survive the widening are the two identity checks the parent requirement grew in review, because both false-render bugs they caught become MORE likely once many windows can claim an engine rather than one.

The second half asks a question nobody has answered: rather than opening another Primary window, could a session be told to orchestrate? The pipeline skills carry no primary-only guard, so the door is already open - what is unknown is whether the claim, the wrappers, the write-isolation hook and the marker all behave from a session clone. That half reports and files rather than fixing, so the indicator ships regardless of the answer.

title: Plan List Status Multi-Select
notes:
Make the plan list's status filter behave like every other status filter in the app.

The pipelines list holds ONE status and matches on equality, so a question as ordinary as "show me the active and the draft plans" cannot be asked. Every other status filter here is multi-select, and the control that does it is already a shared component the requirements view drives - so the work is to delete a hand-rolled single-select and adopt what exists, not to build a second multi-select. A second implementation is how two pages drift apart.

The separate "all" chip goes with it: in a multi-select, all is every chip on, and keeping a dedicated control for it makes two sources of truth for one piece of state.

Default is active plus draft, which is where the interesting decision sits. That set excludes paused - and pausing a plan is a normal, reversible operating state rather than an archival one, unlike completed or aborted. Ship it as specified and someone who has just paused their only plan lands on an empty page with no explanation. So either paused joins the default, or the empty state names the hidden statuses and their counts. A filter that silently hides the thing you were just looking at reads as a bug, whatever the intent.

title: Pause Enforcement
notes:
Replace a promise with infrastructure - the backend half.

The live plan is paused right now and swarm-starts are held back BY AGREEMENT between the user and the Primary. Nothing enforces it: another Primary attaching, or an engine started on the scope, would launch work while both parties believed it paused. Measured, the status field is advisory - the engine never reads it, the derivation never consults it, and the start skill flips a paused plan to active without comment. There is no epic-level pause at all.

Pause means one thing: a scope stops swarm-starting. The engine keeps polling, keeps its heartbeat and keeps reporting regressions and stalls, and must say every cycle that it is paused or a paused scope reads exactly like a dead engine. Running sessions are untouched. Authoring is entirely unaffected - stated explicitly, because an earlier draft wrongly described pause as an authoring mode.

State lives in a status value rather than a new table: the plan already has one, the epic gains one. That is consistent with every other entity here, is multi-machine friendly by being in the shared database, and is read for free by everything already reading the row. The cost is that an epic status cannot say "paused in THAT plan" - accepted deliberately, with the conditions that would justify revisiting it written down.

Multi-tenancy reuses the engine's existing scope-conflict rule rather than inventing a parallel one: pausing one epic leaves its neighbours running, pausing a plan suppresses the epics it contains, two plans never interact.

The start and stop skills change with it under one governing rule - unpausing is the user's decision and nothing else may make it. Start on a paused scope becomes legal and honest rather than silently activating it. Stop leaves pause untouched in both directions.

Split from the visibility half so this is not delayed behind the visualizer work that half must follow. It exposes pause in the composed read so the other half has something to render.

title: Durable Orchestration Reservation
notes:
Make the single-orchestrator guarantee true across machines, and make the holder visible.

The conflict rule itself is correct and needs no change - a whole-plan scope refuses any epic scope on that plan and vice versa, two different epics of one plan run concurrently, two plans never interact. What is wrong is where it is enforced: a machine-local temp directory. Two machines can each claim the same scope, neither sees the other, and both orchestrate the same steps - duplicate sessions on one requirement, which is the exact failure the rule exists to prevent. Liveness is decided by asking whether a pid is alive, which is only answerable locally, so the existing design cannot simply be pointed at a shared store.

The claim protocol needs one correction to its obvious form. Read-if-free then write then read back has a genuine race that gets WIDER across machines, because latency lengthens the window: both sides read free, both write, both read back at the wrong moment and both believe they won. The fix is an atomic insert for the exact scope, so a duplicate of the SAME scope is impossible at the database rather than by timing - plus a deterministic tie-break for the cross-level case a uniqueness constraint cannot express, since a whole-plan claim and an epic claim on that plan are different rows that still conflict. Deciding the winner from stored data both parties can read means both derive the same answer regardless of who read when, and the loser deletes its own row and names the holder.

Liveness is the hard part and is not optional. A durable claim outlives its process, so a lost machine or a closed terminal would block a scope forever with no local pid to interrogate. Heartbeat on the cycle it already runs, a stated staleness threshold comfortably longer than a normal cycle, and reclaiming that is loud about what it took and from where.

Deliberately not merged with pause, though both are scope-keyed and durable: a reservation is a live claim tied to a running process and reclaimed on staleness; a pause is a user intention that outlives every process and must never be reclaimed.

title: Pause Visibility
notes:
Render what pause records, on the surfaces where a user actually looks.

A red or green bubble immediately left of every epic name on its band - readable at any zoom without hovering or reading text - plus a paused indicator on the plan list and plan detail, and, subtlest of the three, eligibility surfaces that distinguish eligible-and-suppressed from eligible. That last one is the most likely to be skipped and the most damaging to omit: eligibility is derived and will keep saying yes, so suppression has to render ALONGSIDE it rather than replacing it, or a user reads a paused plan as about to run.

Split from the enforcement half deliberately. Enforcement touches no UI at all, while everything here lands on the plan visualizer - which is serialised behind the epic-label work on the same rectangle. Bundled, a backend correctness fix replacing a mental convention would have waited four sessions of unrelated polish before it could start.

Ordered after the epic-label work for the same reason that work was grouped: the bubble is width the label did not have before, and the zero-overlap invariant has to be re-checked against the final chip rather than one about to move. Colours come from the palette rather than hardcoded, and face the same dark-panel test as every other band colour - a status signal that reads as muddy is worse than no signal.

title: Step Editor Page
notes:
The step editor, built second - copying the pattern the epic editor establishes rather than inventing a second dialect of it.

Same navigation level, same page shape, same relationship to an existing editing surface. It shares a navigation tree and a route table with its siblings, so it follows rather than runs beside them.

title: Feature Editor Page
notes:
The feature editor, last of the three - by which point the pattern is settled twice over and this page is the cheapest of them.

Same navigation level and route table as its siblings, so it follows them rather than running beside them.

title: Canvas: Hover Datacards
notes:
The hover datacards are the only place a reader learns what a bead, a bare id or a dashed box is - the canvas draws identifiers on purpose, because a plan title is many times the width of the column it hangs under, and that puts the whole explanatory burden on the hover.

Today the step name does not listen at all, so hovering the words falls through to the dashed batch rectangle beneath and produces the wrong card. Both cards also lead with the wrong thing: one with an identifier and the name buried in a field, the other the reverse. Both should lead with the name, and the requirement card must answer how work will be executed rather than only what it is called.

Follows the L1 gate deliberately. The hit region this adds to the step name must answer to the SAME level condition that pass introduced, or it becomes an invisible hotspot over undrawn text.

One open question is written into the requirement rather than guessed at: whether the batch rectangle should lose hover to what is drawn above it, or win it. A one-line flip either way, and only the user can settle it.

title: Canvas: Reset And HUD Cleanup
notes:
Clear the bottom-right corner of the canvas and give Reset its real meaning.

The pan-and-zoom hint bubble goes entirely - those gestures are discovered in a second by anyone who touches the canvas, and a permanent caption costs corner space forever. Reset means FACTORY DEFAULT: fully zoomed out, whole vertical extent visible. Confirm the current default actually does that rather than assuming, because a reset that lands somewhere the user still has to zoom out from is not a reset.

The follow-through is the real work. Both chips live in one stack marked as viewer chrome, and that marking is load-bearing: the gesture filters consult it so a mousedown on a control, or in the gap between chips, does not start a pan. Emptying the stack means removing it and every exclusion that existed only for it, while leaving the key's own intact. And before deleting the level chip, check it is not the sole indicator that a level is pinned.

Third in the canvas chain, and it clears the corner the final pass then has to place a control into.

title: Canvas: Level Control Placement
notes:
Where the semantic level control belongs - and the one canvas change that needs the user before it can proceed.

Last in the chain, because it depends on the corner being cleared and because it carries an unresolved question. The requirement was re-grounded against the merged code and found a direct conflict with itself: the control was moved INTO the key by the polish pass on purpose, and the code records a measured reason - it got the control off a header row that had grown past 2300px of natural content. This asks for the reverse.

The session's FIRST act is to raise that with the user, measurement in hand, rather than picking a side. Moving it to the header anyway is legitimate, but then the header overflow becomes in-scope work rather than something inherited - a wrapped or scrolling header row is not an acceptable outcome.

Also corrected in the re-grounding: these are not zoom in/out buttons. The control selects which marks are drawn at all, so nothing about transforms or scale extents applies to it. And the key is now a structured multi-channel block rather than a flat pill, so re-proportioning it is a larger job than the original wording implied.

title: Orchestrator Lesson Ten
notes:
One more orchestrator lesson, learned twice in an afternoon after the first nine were already groomed - and both times the cost was a hand-repair minutes before a launch.

A step holding N requirements is one command that spawns N SESSIONS, not one session working through N requirements. Design rule 2 groups requirements that may run CONCURRENTLY behind a single gate; it says nothing about authorship, and reading "launch unit" as "one worker" is the trap the vocabulary sets.

Both instances were caught only because the launch line was read before being acted on. Three editor pages seated together on the reasoning that one author gives one pattern would have started three sessions writing to the same navigation tree and route table. Four canvas requirements seated together included two whose own text describes them as editing the same three lines with an interaction between them - a hit region added to a label another requirement stops drawing.

So: requirements sharing a step must be safe to start simultaneously, because that is what happens. Two requirements needing the same author must become ONE requirement - no plan structure expresses "one session, two requirements". Two that merely must not overlap get a dependency edge.

The lesson also corrects the absorb branch of the existing absorb-chain-separate rule, which is the sentence that produced both errors: absorb means merge into one REQUIREMENT, not put two requirements in one step. And the better justification usually appears once the chain exists - the editor pages ended up sequenced so the later pages copy a shipped one rather than inventing a parallel dialect, which outlives the conflict that prompted it.

title: Orchestrator Lesson Eleven
notes:
The eleventh orchestrator lesson, and the first one paid for with the plan running unattended rather than caught before a launch.

A `deployed` requirement means nobody is watching. So an instruction inside one to raise something with the user before proceeding does not produce a considered answer - it produces a session parked in planning, holding everything chained behind it. Measured here: a pop-up requirement carrying a deliberate open question sat for about three hours while a sibling launched ninety minutes later reached active in eight and a half minutes and finished.

The intent was right and the mechanism wrong. Flagging a real ambiguity beats guessing silently; the mistake is doing it at an autonomy level defined by absence.

So an open question needs either a stated default the session may act on, or a coordination type that stops for a human - deliberately, never neither. Prefer the default, because most of these are placement or wording or a one-line flip, and a report saying which way it went costs one read while a stalled chain costs everything behind it. Choose the default by asymmetry rather than taste: when a requirement conflicts with a recent decision somebody made on evidence, default to preserving that decision, because undoing it unattended is the worse error. And where no default is safe - a schema shape, a security posture - the requirement simply is not deployed, and saying so while authoring is the whole job.

This refines rather than contradicts the existing autonomy rule, which already handles a requirement that is ENTIRELY an open question. The gap is the requirement that is mostly actionable and contains just one blocking question - which turns out to be enough to strand it.

title: Statusline Marker Pid Match
notes:
A consumer broke the moment the durable reservation shipped, and it broke into silence.

The start skill verifies it actually won a scope before writing the status-line marker, by matching the pid on the engine's START line against the pid in the scope registry. That was correct while START carried one pid field. The reservation work added a second - a terminal pid, which is exactly the identity it was asked to carry - and the pattern `pid=[0-9]+` matches inside `terminal_pid=` too. Two values come back, the comparison fails, the marker is never written.

The failure mode is the reason this is worth a requirement rather than a one-line commit. A comparison that can now only be FALSE takes the same branch a genuinely REFUSED launch takes. So an orchestrator that legitimately owns its scope displays no orchestration and looks identical to one that lost the race - which is the exact confusion the check exists to prevent.

Nothing was wrong with adding the field. The defect is a consumer parsing a structured line with a pattern loose enough to match a field that did not exist yet, and then using the result where failure is silent. That suggests the third scope item: the engine's output line is a contract with readers, and this is the second time an added field has broken a downstream parse in this feature.

title: Requirement Epic Linkage
notes:
Tell a requirement page which epic it belongs to, and let the reader click through.

The page says nothing today about where the requirement sits in the plan, even though epic is the top of the hierarchy and the unit orchestration is scoped by. A bordered, captioned box to the right of AI Settings, styled as its sibling - the same fieldset and legend treatment so the caption sits on the border line - carrying the epic name as a link.

Read-only and completely so: no add, update, delete or inline edit. Matching the AI Settings LOOK is the requirement; matching its edit behaviour is not, and the page's edit-in-place pattern should stay out of this box.

The interesting half is that the value is DERIVED. A requirement has no epic column - the epic is reached through its feature, and either link can be absent. No feature means no epic, which is a legitimate and common state rather than an error, so the box has to say so plainly instead of rendering an empty rectangle that reads as a bug.

One thing to decide rather than assume: the page holds a feature id but no feature or epic title, and the right way to resolve those is a question about what the page already fetches. Widening an existing projection is the right trade; adding a whole-table read per requirement page to render one label is not.

title: Epic Link To Plan Location
notes:
Add a second link: where this epic sits in the plan.

The linkage box shipped correctly and opens the epic itself. That answers "what is this epic". A second link answers a different and equally useful question - "where does this sit in the plan" - landing on the canvas with that epic's band in view. Both stay; the box gains an affordance rather than changing destination, and the two have to be distinguishable before clicking or two bare anchors on one name is worse than one.

It is not a one-line swap, which is the whole reason it is its own requirement. The plan route takes a PIPELINE id, and the requirement page has no idea which pipeline hosts its epic - an epic is seated through its steps, and nothing on that page walks that far. And the plan view reads exactly one query param today, so an epic deep-link parameter has to be introduced and consumed.

Two cases the resolution must answer honestly, neither an error: an epic in NO pipeline has no location, so omit only the plan link and leave the epic link untouched; an epic in SEVERAL needs a deterministic rule, and the composed-read resolver already has a tie-break worth reusing rather than inventing a second one.

The landing itself is wiring rather than building - epic view centering shipped the same day, so the deep-link consumes an existing behaviour. Through the zoom behaviour rather than by setting transform state, and waiting for layout rather than firing against an empty canvas.

The constraint carried forward from the shipped work: no whole-table read on the requirement page. That box was deliberately built on targeted single-row reads instead of the plan view's label dictionaries, and resolving a pipeline must not undo that.

title: Navbar Plan Entities As L3
notes:
Put the plan's entities under the plan.

Epics, Features and Steps sit as flat L2 siblings of Pipelines today, which reads as though they were peers of it. They are its contents - an epic, a feature and a step are the plan's own entities - so they belong beneath it, collapsible, the way Sessions already carries Starts, Completes and Undos.

The mechanism is not the work. The session-expansion requirement shipped the L3 concept earlier the same day and is its only user so far: an L2 link carries a children array, the sidebar renders them indented behind a toggle, the group starts closed, and landing on an L3 route from a bookmark opens its parent. This is a navConfig edit that reuses all of it. Depth is deliberately one level and the code says so - generalising the mechanism while in there is the temptation to resist.

What needs actual thought is smaller and easier to miss. The three should read in hierarchy order rather than alphabetically. The flatten helper exists because any consumer iterating the nav list while ignoring children silently loses every L3 - and a silent drop looks like a missing menu item rather than a bug, so every consumer wants auditing now that a second parent has children. Icon-only mode has no room for a toggle and handles children differently; whatever Sessions does there, these must match. And there are two things called Features in this sidebar - confirm which one is being nested and that the other is untouched, because two Features entries at different depths would be worse than the flat arrangement being replaced.

title: Epic Label: Counts
notes:
Show progress next to the name - met over total for that scope - behind an on/off toggle, on both the epic band label and wherever a plan is named.

Second in the label chain, and it goes before the sticky-name work for a concrete reason: THIS IS THE PASS THAT CHANGES LABEL WIDTH. The label participates in the zero-overlap contract the layout tests assert, so widening it is the geometry event the collision handling downstream has to be built against. Doing it after sticky names would mean the sticky work verified collisions at widths that were about to change.

The counts are derived at zero cost from rows the composed read already carries, and belong with the other derived values rather than computed in the component. No new gateway read.

Two questions to decide rather than assume, because both change the number a reader sees: whether container requirements count at all - they are excluded from a step's gating set, so counting them would make a completable plan never read complete - and whether work that is terminal-but-not-met stays in the denominator. Say which was chosen; a plan permanently short of its total must not read as a stall.

The example given was ambiguous - the live epic is itself titled "Pipeline", so "pipeline names" resolves to either the plan title or that epic's band label. Both are the same computation; build both, and the band label first if only one.

title: Epic Label: Sticky Names
notes:
Keep at least three epic names on screen while moving through a tall plan: the bands immediately above and below the one in view hold their names at the viewport edges, the way a date header sticks in a scrolling list, and stay clickable so clicking up through the stack becomes how you move between epics.

Last in the label chain, and it is last because it is the pass that has to reason about COLLISIONS - and by now the label's final geometry exists. The palette settled the colours and the counts settled the width, so this work verifies overlap against what the label will actually be rather than against a width about to change underneath it.

Names must not collide as bands pass each other. The whole point is legibility, and two labels overlapping at a boundary is worse than one label missing. Its rectangles belong in the same label set the zero-overlap invariant already covers, not in a second untested class of text.

Zoom is a pure transform, so nothing here may trigger a relayout on a level change.

title: Engine Edge Log Retention
notes:
Restarting the engine destroys the record of what the previous engine did.

The start skill launches with a truncating redirect to a fixed, scope-keyed path. An engine self-terminates at its wall-clock budget and gets restarted to keep sequencing - normal, expected, twice in one day on one scope. Each restart truncated the file, taking two engines' worth of edges with it: every launch, state change, regression, stall and verdict across roughly twelve hours.

It is the remaining half of a defect already half-fixed. The earlier fix addressed a SECOND launch truncating a LIVE engine's file mid-run; this is a sequential restart truncating a DEAD one. No race, no conflict, no refusal - so none of that fix's guards apply, and the same fixed path with the same redirect loses the same data.

Why it matters more than a lost log usually would: the engine is deliberately stdout-only for edges. Sessions record their own work and the plan records its own state, but the ORCHESTRATION - what was commanded and when, what re-announced because a launch never took, what was reported and never acted on - exists only in this file. The resync skill's replay step reads it to tell a re-attaching Primary what it missed, and after a restart there is nothing to replay.

Two directions with different costs, and the requirement states both rather than picking: appending preserves everything but grows unbounded, and a per-run filename keeps runs separate but breaks the fixed path the Monitor arms on and the statusline resolves. Either way a restart must not silently discard the previous record - and if a bound is introduced, exceeding it has to be visible rather than a quiet drop.

title: Partial Update Echo Integrity
notes:
The verification discipline may not be verifying anything.

A partial requirement update passed one field and left another - never mentioned by the caller - holding a different value in the database than the response reported. The echo said the pre-call value and passed; a fresh read hours later disagreed, with the update timestamp pointing at that same call and nothing since. Two reads agreed.

Either the write changed a field it was not asked to, or the returned row is not the row that was stored. Both are serious, they are not exclusive, and which one it is has not been established - so this is an investigation with a fix attached, not a fix with a rationale attached. The obvious explanation is only half an explanation: a documented default exists, but the value landed somewhere the default does not point, so stopping at "probably defaults" would be stopping too early.

The reason it justifies this weight is the standing echo-verification rule itself. Never fire-and-forget, confirm the returned row - the rule exists because a silently-failed write is invisible. If a response can differ from storage, the rule produces false confidence rather than protection, and everything verified by it is unverified in fact. On the day this surfaced, roughly twenty requirement writes plus every pipeline step mutation went through that pattern in one orchestration run.

So the scope runs past the fix: establish the mechanism from the code, check whether the sibling writers share the shape, audit which rows were actually altered rather than which could have been, and cover it with a test that reads FRESH after a partial update - because a test asserting on the response would reproduce the blind spot exactly.

title: Reasoned Non-Delivery Instruction
notes:
Name and forbid the failure where a real obstacle becomes permission not to build what was asked.

The shape is specific. A requirement asks for X. Investigation surfaces a genuine obstacle - a prior decision, a measurement, a constraint. The obstacle is treated as AUTHORITY rather than as work. Something adjacent to X ships, or X ships where nobody sees it. The completion report explains the reasoning clearly and reads as diligence.

Only the third step is wrong; the rest is correct behaviour, which is exactly what makes this expensive. Sloppy non-delivery is obvious. Reasoned non-delivery survives review because the reasoning is genuine and challenging it means re-litigating an argument that sounds right.

Two measured examples, both authored by the Primary AI on the same day, both shipped, both invisible to the person who asked. A control was to move to the header; a prior session had moved it out with a measurement attached, so the requirement was given a default instructing the session not to move it - with the correct option written into the same requirement and then not taken. And a met-against-total progress count was to be visible on the plan; it shipped behind a toggle defaulting off, present and correct and unseeable.

So the rules: an obstacle is work rather than authority, and solving it is in scope by default. Nothing already in the codebase outranks the ask - a prior implementation tells you the cost, not the decision. A session choosing without the user present defaults TOWARD the deliverable and reports the cost. A feature nobody can see is not delivered. A title promising what the body declines is a lie in the plan. And the escape hatch is asking at authoring time, not deciding at build time.

The self-check matters most, because this is invisible from the inside: would the person who asked, looking at the running system, see the thing they described?

title: Deliver The Declined Deliverables
notes:
Deliver the two things that were asked for, shipped as something else, and are therefore not in the product.

Reviewed against the merged code, and the two are not in the same state. The level control never moved - it still renders from the key, and the header file imports it without rendering it, which is the visible trace of a move started and abandoned. The counts, by contrast, were built correctly on both surfaces and simply default to off, so the person who asked to see the numbers does not see them.

So the remediation differs. One is a real move with real work attached: the header row had grown past 2300px, which is why an earlier pass took the control out, and that measurement is exactly what makes this a job rather than a one-liner. The overflow is IN SCOPE - it is what the move requires, not a reason to skip it, and the header must stay one row. The other is a default flip, with the note that if defaulting on strains the header, that is the same overflow the first half is already solving rather than a second excuse to stay hidden.

One requirement because both land in the same two files and both turn on the same header-width question; two sessions would contend for the same rows and could reach opposite conclusions.

Stated plainly in the requirement because it is the point: this is remediation of requirements that were authored to decline their own deliverable, so declining again is not available. If either half proves genuinely impossible that is a blocking question for the user, not a default to fall back on.

title: Plan Visualizer Polish #2
notes:
A second polish pass over the plan visualizer, with the live Darwin plan loaded.

Held behind the visualizer work in flight rather than run beside it. Two sessions are in that component right now - the remediation moving the level control into the header and solving the header overflow, and the sticky epic names - and a polish pass is precisely the kind of work that touches everything they are touching. It goes last so it polishes the finished surface rather than one being rebuilt underneath it.

The requirement is not yet startable, and the reason is worth recording rather than discovering at launch. The FIRST visualizer polish carried a concept list - scroll pane, epic title collisions, readable default size, a step-width option, navbar separation, next-step highlighting - six concrete items that made "polish" a scope rather than an instruction to use judgement. This one currently carries a single sentence. An autonomous session given that would either invent the list or stall, and inventing it is the failure the non-delivery instruction exists to name.

So it stays in authoring until the user supplies the concepts. That is the one input nobody else can provide - polish is a judgement about what looks wrong to the person who looks at it.

title: Wakeup Guard Coverage
notes:
Stop needless wakeups being armed, rather than cleaning them up after they fire.

A worker waiting on a code-reviewer subagent armed a wakeup at 180 seconds as a fallback. The subagent reply is harness-tracked and notified on its own, so the timer was never needed; it was never cancelled, and it fired after the session had merged, deployed, closed its requirement, destroyed its worktree and printed a terminal completion - putting text past a boundary whose whole contract is that nothing follows it.

A guard already exists for this family and did not catch it, which is the useful part. It blocks an arm when an outstanding background Bash task is present, and it has two precise holes. Its detector only recognises background Bash, so a subagent or a Monitor - equally harness-tracked, equally auto-notifying - is invisible to it. And it never inspects the delay at all, so a 180-second arm passes even though the tool's own contract prohibits short-interval polling of harness-tracked work and puts genuine fallbacks at 1200 seconds or more.

So: teach the detector the other start/notification pairs, and give the guard an opinion about the delay - blocking a short arm unless the caller states on the record that it is watching external state the harness cannot see. Not a blanket floor, because that case is real and documented; the floor is what separates waiting on something that will announce itself from watching something that will not.

Cleaning up at closeout was considered and deliberately set aside. The fix belongs at the arming end: a wakeup never created cannot survive a boundary, and a cleanup step would be a second mechanism maintaining state the first should not have produced.

title: Concurrency Ceiling
notes:
Set this Mac's concurrent orchestrated-session ceiling to 20, and stop the orchestrator defaulting to a number nobody chose.

Fifteen concurrent sessions ran clean here, so twenty is a measured step rather than a guess. The interesting half is not the number, though - it is that the current default of 4 is the skill's own literal, chosen by no one, and that the cap is enforced by the Primary AI while the engine merely records it. Those two facts met on 2026-08-02: the live run record said ten, the skill text said four, and work was held against the wrong one. A number that lives in prose and in a run record at the same time will disagree with itself eventually.

So the fix is the default AND the source of truth. Raise the ceiling, chase down every place the old figure is stated, and make the Primary read the cap it enforces from the run record rather than from the skill it happens to be reading. The per-machine question is deliberately left as a judgement with a stated preference for the simple literal, because a migration to hold one integer for a machine nobody orchestrates on is a cost looking for a reason.

Leaves the launcher separation alone: the engine emits, the Primary launches, and nothing here changes that.

title: Pipeline Skill Refinement
notes:
Optimize the Pipeline skill surface against four named goals - save time, save tokens, grow the deterministic core, improve stability or function - with a hard bar attached: every change names its goal and its material benefit, and a refactor that is merely tidier is rejected. Finding little worth changing and saying so is a successful outcome here.

The highest-value axis is the third. Skill prose is interpreted by an LLM on every invocation, which means it can be interpreted differently twice and cannot be unit-tested; a script does the same thing every time. Wherever a step is mechanical, it belongs in a script the skill calls.

The order of work matters as much as the work. A test baseline is taken FIRST, gaps closed, and the whole suite proved green BEFORE anything is refined - a baseline taken afterward is not a baseline, and refining on a red one makes every later result unattributable. The same suite is then the instrument for judging the changes, with anything genuinely untestable named as such rather than blurred into the word "tested". Design changes end up in the architect's documents, because a design change living only in code is one the next session will not find.

It runs last because it optimizes a surface that several sibling requirements are still changing; starting earlier would tune something that then moves underneath it. It is also the expensive one - multiple agent passes over a large surface - so it is deliberately placed where it cannot hold anything else up.

Grounded in a real 30-requirement run rather than theory: the transcript, the engine's run record and the session telemetry are all evidence about which steps were slow, re-done, or got wrong.

title: Remove Pipelined Notice
notes:
Take the pipelined-exclusion notice off the SwarmStartCard.

The card explains, under its launch chips, that some requirements are hidden because a pipeline step carries them. The user sees this card constantly and does not want the sentence. That is the whole of the ask.

The care is entirely in what must NOT change. The exclusion itself is load-bearing: plan-sequenced work stays off the launch chips and out of the counts, because putting it back would let a bulk launch start a step ahead of its dependencies. So this removes the explanation and leaves the behaviour untouched — if the diff changes which rows are listed or what a chip counts, it went wrong.

The notice also has a tail. The hidden-count it renders is fed by a map, which is fed by half of a tally function's return value, and nothing else consumes any of it. Leaving that computed and unread would be residue of exactly the kind that makes a later reader think the feature is still present, so the chain goes with the sentence, along with the tests that assert on a return value that will no longer exist.

Stated in the requirement because a session will otherwise find it and hesitate: the notice was added deliberately, with a written argument that a silently-shrinking list reads as a bug.
