That reasoning was sound. The user has since lived with the result and decided against it, which is theirs to decide — the recorded rationale says what the removal costs, not whether to do it.

title: Concurrency Cap Eradication
notes: The per-run concurrency knob was tuned three times and never became safe; removing the knob is the fix, so this must land after the refinement pass that last touched the same skill prose and contract test.

title: Layout Cell Collision
notes:
A timed layout can put two beads on one (band, column, lane) cell, so their labels draw over each other and the layout module breaks its oldest invariant. Found by fuzzing during an unrelated review; pre-existing, and not caused by the ruler work that surfaced it.

The requirement carries a root-cause HYPOTHESIS rather than a finding, and says so: the dep-adjacent lane insertion path is the only lane assignment that never re-checks the lane it picks. Confirm or refute it before fixing — the alternative explanation is a column floor collapsing two chains that a pure depth axis kept apart.

Why it stayed invisible is the useful part. The assertion that would have caught it already existed, but its fixture was rebuilt from a model whose rows carried no pipeline key, so the rebuild filtered every row away and sixteen plan-scale tests asserted over an empty array. That fixture has since been repaired and guarded, and on the repaired fixture this defect does not reproduce — which is why a fuzz corpus is part of the deliverable rather than a nicety.

title: Guard Message Stream
notes:
Three PreToolUse guards write their block message to stdout and exit 2, and a PreToolUse hook relays only stderr on exit 2 — so the caller sees a bare 'No stderr output' line and nothing else. Measured on a live worker, which recovered by guessing.

It matters more than the one-line fix suggests. Each of those messages exists to TEACH: it names the allowlist, the wrapper policy, or the override token that is the lawful way forward. A guard whose refusal cannot be read is a wall rather than a guard, so the whole remediation half of each was dead from the day it was written.

A reference implementation already exists — one guard was corrected earlier with a single redirect placed before its verdict block. The test assertion is the load-bearing half: the existing suites capture with 2>&1, which cannot tell the two streams apart, so without a per-stream assertion the fix rots back silently.

title: Status Write Timestamp Parity
notes:
One column, two writers, two behaviours: a status change made through the MCP path re-derives all three lifecycle timestamps, and the same change made from the UI writes the status alone.

Filed at its honest weight. A production sweep found ZERO damaged rows — every terminal requirement carries its completion stamp — so this is a latent inconsistency rather than observed damage. The reason it has not bitten is that transitions currently run overwhelmingly through MCP, which is a property of habit and not of the code.

The requirement now carries a written default for its one open design question, chosen by asymmetry so an unattended session need not stop to ask. Both this and the notice removal edit the same card component, so they must not run at the same time.

title: Re-Announce Marker Survival
notes:
The re-announce marker is what tells a Primary that a repeated launch line means the work never started, rather than the engine looping. Losing it inverts the meaning of the one line that reports a missed launch, so a Primary can reasonably ignore exactly the line it must act on.

Measured with no pause anywhere in the reproduction: a step that goes foreign and returns loses the marker, while the identical expiry without the ownership change keeps it. The deferral itself is correct and stays; only the annotation is lost, and the backoff is unaffected.

The hazard is in the fix rather than the defect. The engine deliberately holds almost no state between cycles, so anything carried forward here has to stay bounded by the same forgetting discipline every other store of its class has, or it becomes the latch that design forbids. Both this and the cap eradication edit the engine module, so they must not run at the same time.

title: Batch Render Vertical Space
notes:
A user screenshot of the live plan showed a long dashed hairline running down an otherwise empty
band from a batch letter to its box, and uneven spacing between the batch members inside it. Both
halves were measured against the live plan before the requirement was written, so the session
starts from numbers rather than from the picture.

Chained behind the layout cell-collision work rather than run beside it: both edit the lane
placement in the same layout module, and the cell-collision requirement carries a hypothesis about
the same dep-adjacent insertion path this one suspects. Running them together would put two authors
in those lines at once; running this one second lets it re-measure on the shipped fix and, if that
fix already closed the lane half, deliver only what is left.

title: Orchestration Status Report
notes:
One scripted report, produced the same way every time, so a status answer stops being an LLM's summary of whatever it happened to read. The plan already has a rule that anything mechanical belongs in a script a test can reach — this is that rule applied to the thing the user asks for most often.

The report must carry what the run WILL DO, not only what it has done: the plans in flight and the launches that would go out immediately. A status report that omits the pending launches answers a different question from the one being asked.

Progressive disclosure is a requirement of the output, not a style note — the full telemetry has to be reachable without the headline drowning in it. It edits the same skill prose and the same orchestration scripts as the cap eradication, so the two must not run at the same time.

title: Pause Response Line
notes:
A pause receipt ran to thirty-four lines for one changed bit. The user wants one sentence, and the sentence already has a house form — every swarm lifecycle skill ends with a single title-case summary line, and that convention predates this by months.

Both halves have to move together: the script prints the receipt and the skill prose then instructs the assistant to repeat and annotate it, so fixing either alone leaves the verbosity in the other. An error still explains itself freely — the terseness is the SUCCESS path only, which is where essentially every invocation lands.

title: Visualizer Viewport Restore
notes:
Returning to the plan visualizer from any drill-through drops the user back at a default view, so the position they navigated away from has to be found again by hand every time.

The ask is explicitly for EVERY return path rather than the three the user happened to hit, so the shape is one restore mechanism the page owns, not a patch at each call site. It shares its component with the polish pass already in flight and with the key placement that follows, which is why all three are sequenced rather than run together.

It also carries a grooming half: the title-bar patterns in the NON-pipeline visualizers are the better exemplars, and the deviations here are the thing to name.

title: Visualizer Key Placement
notes:
The key sits where the epics flow — down and to the right — so it competes with the content it exists to explain. Moving it to the bottom centre takes it out of that path.

The hide/unhide control is the second half and the easier one to under-deliver: it is meant to be MORE prominent, lighter, and possibly larger, and the size call is the implementer's to make rather than a question to bring back.

It edits the same visualizer component as the viewport restore, so it follows it.

title: Epic Name Pinning
notes:
An epic name is supposed to belong to its band's rectangle, and today it does not: the obstacle-avoidance pass slides it sideways over the step field, where it misreads as labelling whatever it is sitting on, and panning deep into a tall band loses the name altogether because placement is confined to the band's own lane and drops the chip when that lane leaves the viewport.

The rule the user stated is a single one — the name sits at the top-left of its rectangle intersected with the visible area — and it replaces an earlier spec inside this same requirement that called for one shared column at the plan's left edge. That earlier spec was written, checked against the running product and rejected; the requirement carries both so no reader rebuilds the version that was turned down.

The width metric is the trap the module header warns about — an under-measured chip width corrupts every geometric decision downstream — which is why the font and its measurement are explicitly out of scope.

Autonomy was lowered to stop for a manual review: the user wants to polish this one live against the running plan rather than accept it unattended.

It rewrites the same module the polish pass and the lane-collision fix are in, so it cannot run alongside either.

title: Date Header Sticky
notes:
The date header is anchored to the top item in the stack, so scrolling the plan takes the timeline's own axis off screen and leaves every bead below it unreadable against anything.

The sticky mechanism it needs already exists in the swarm visualizer's day headers — pin, get pushed up by the next one, drop when fully behind — and copying it is cheaper and more consistent than a second implementation beside it.

It follows the epic-name column because both want the top strip of the viewport, and only one can own it. The requirement now carries the layering decision as a stated default so an unattended session settles it rather than stalling on it.

title: Pause Line Names Scope
notes:
A confirmation that reads identically for every scope confirms nothing — the user paused an epic and had to ask whether the right thing had been paused, which is the entire cost of this bug.

The cause is worth carrying, because it is a class rather than a typo: the requirement that introduced the terse line illustrated its SHAPE with two sample sentences, and those samples were implemented as literal constants. The same pass then wrote the generalisation into both skills as a rule forbidding the scope name, which is why fixing the string alone would leave the defect documented as intended behaviour.

The terseness itself was correct and is not being reopened. One line, no receipt relay, nothing else added back — the scope's name is the only thing this restores.

The resolver already prints the type and quoted title and re-reads the row to verify, so the name is in hand when the report is written and costs no extra call.

title: Target Resolver Token Extraction
notes:
A command refused to find a thing it was printing three lines below the refusal. That is a grammar hole rather than a user error, and it is broken identically in all three commands because they share one front door.

The fix replaces positional parsing with token extraction, which is FEWER moving parts than what it removes: today every accepted form is a rung on a ladder, and any form the ladder does not enumerate degrades silently into a literal title search. One extraction pass plus one search means new forms stop needing new code.

Two guards are load-bearing and easy to lose. An epic is titled 'Pipeline', so a bare type keyword with nothing else must stay a NAME rather than becoming a qualifier; and live titles begin with type keywords, so a scoped query has to fall back to the full unstripped string rather than replacing it. Both need fixture-backed tests, because a fix here without them is one rename away from reverting unnoticed.

The requirement also records a REJECTED alternative — handing the parse to the calling model — with its reasoning, so the decision is not re-litigated by whoever reads this next.

It rewrites the same two functions in the same module the concurrency-cap eradication is removing arguments from, so the two cannot run at the same time.

title: Telemetry Run Nine Retro-Fix
notes: Mechanical follow-through on a correction that could not be applied from inside the session that made it possible: a worker may not restart the shared daemon, so the tool it had just shipped was unreachable to it. The stored prose is the measurement's public face, and leaving known errors in it costs more than the fix.

title: Steerable Subagent Delegation
notes: A delegation that holds the main loop leaves the user a choice between waiting and destroying the work in flight, which is not steering. Treated as a harness responsibility rather than a rule to remember, because a rule that is forgotten silently produces exactly the unsteerable session it was written to prevent.

title: Agents Registry Doc Correction
notes: Re-ground the agents-registry documentation on what the registry actually serves, after a refactor moved the model out from under it. Sequenced behind the common-band authoring work because that work changes the very band this documents -- correcting it first would re-stale it on arrival. Its own text carries a struck claim from an earlier revision; the correction notice stays, because a reader who saw the wrong version needs to know it was withdrawn.

title: Ownership Edge Scoping
notes:
Two different epics of one plan are designed to orchestrate concurrently from two machines, so an epic-scoped run narrating another epic's churn is one tenant reporting another's activity as though it were its own — to a Primary that will then reason about it. That makes it a multi-tenancy defect rather than a verbosity one.

The engine already committed to the right principle and already has the predicate for it; one emission sits above the guard that applies it. So the work is routing an existing check through an existing helper, not introducing a concept.

The trap is that an ownership change is the one event that can change whether a step is in scope, so the obvious filter suppresses exactly the two cases that matter — gaining a step and losing one mid-flight. The predicate has to consider both sides of the move.

The second trap is quieter: the remembered epic is committed inside the emission today, so filtering the message without keeping the bookkeeping leaves a stale label that corrupts the NEXT comparison. Filter what is said, never what is recorded.

The full-plan load stays — dep edges cross epic boundaries and a slice load would leave gates dangling. Only the observation narrows.

It edits the same cycle-diff function as the re-announce marker fix, so the two cannot run at the same time.

title: Ownership Deferral Bypass
notes:
Three defects from one category error: the re-announce fact belongs to a STEP, and the engine carries it as a scalar attached to a LINE.

Two of the three are lost annotations. The first is not — the batch path can command a step on the very cycle the engine prints that it is NOT launching it, so an epic-scoped engine gaining a step commands work another epic's orchestrator may be commanding at the same instant. That is the exact outcome the ownership deferral exists to prevent, it reproduces on a first-ever announcement with no debounce involved, and it was measured rather than reasoned.

The narrow marker fix that preceded this declared the deferral out of scope and left it untouched; this is where that decision is revisited, so the earlier call is not treated as a standing answer.

Scope was left open between a mandatory part and two optional ones. It has been decided in the requirement rather than left for an unattended session to settle, along with a stated fallback if the unifying shape does not reach all three.

One existing test pins the current behaviour deliberately and has to be updated rather than removed — the kind of thing a refactor deletes without noticing.

It edits the same ownership handling in the cycle diff as the edge-scoping work, so the two cannot run at the same time.

title: Pause State In Run Record
notes:
A paused orchestration currently looks exactly like a live one on the status line, which is the same class of problem pause visibility was filed for elsewhere: a suppressed scope that goes quiet is indistinguishable from a dead one.

The producer side is nearly free and that is the argument for doing it this way. The engine already computes pause every cycle and already rewrites the record every cycle, and the consumer already parses that record with jq on every render — so the fact travels on machinery that exists, with no new file, no new process and nothing added to render time. Any design where the consumer asks the database is wrong, because it runs on every render.

The subtle half is what the field MEANS. A whole-plan run with one paused epic is still launching work, and reporting it as paused would be false — that is the case most likely to be got wrong, and it is why the field answers 'is this scope launching nothing' rather than 'is anything paused'.

Only the producer is in scope. The consumer lives in the user-config repo, which a worker's write isolation refuses, so it is a different executor and a separate requirement.

It edits the same engine module as the ownership work, so the two cannot run at the same time.

title: Deferred Counts As Done
notes:
An epic band renders Complete while its own label says one short, because the count and the state machine answer the same question two different ways in the same file — the constant listing the terminal statuses sits forty lines from a bare string compare that ignores it.

So this is a consistency fix rather than a policy change: the count adopts the set the derivation already uses, and nothing about doneness is redefined.

The hazard is the word 'terminal' appearing in a second place that is deliberately different. The closeout gate excludes deferred on purpose, because postponed work must not let a session close claiming it finished — one asks whether an epic has outstanding work, the other whether a session did what it was given. Unifying them would be a real regression wearing the look of a cleanup.

Two implementations have to move together: the daemon's and the browser's are deliberate duplicates that cannot share code, and the shared conformance corpus is the only thing stopping them drifting.

title: Next-Up Halo At Overview
notes:
The one question a plan view is opened to answer is what runs next, and at the level people open it in, the mark that answers it is not there — while the key goes on advertising it.

The irony is recorded in the code: this halo was ADDED because a thin ring read as nothing at Overview, and its comment claims it draws at every zoom level. That is true of the draw call and false of the result, because the mark is specified in world units and everything world-space is multiplied by the zoom. A filled bead survives that scaling; a dashed outline does not.

Two documented constraints have to survive the fix, and both are easy to trample. The radius is bounded by the text above and below the bead rather than chosen for impact, and the dash exists because only a quarter-pixel separates this ring from the bead's own — so form, not distance, is what stops the two reading as one thick edge. A solid halo, or a fatter one, breaks the thing it was meant to fix.

The stated cause is analysis rather than a measurement, and the requirement says so: confirm it against the live canvas before writing the fix.

title: Epic Label Legibility Floor
notes:
A production screenshot shows the whole plan with no epic names on it. Zooming out is exactly when a reader needs to know which region they are looking at, and it is the one time the label is guaranteed absent.

Both symptoms — names shrinking to unreadable, then disappearing — are two branches of the same four lines, and neither is a mistake. The floor is applied to the BOX rather than the FONT, so the smallest legal box yields a font under seven pixels, and one line earlier a lane too short for that box drops the chip outright. Both are documented choices; the user is overruling them rather than reporting a defect.

So the work inverts the constraint: floor the font, derive the box, and stop dropping. That reverses a decision made to keep the epic name off the first row of step labels, and the requirement says so plainly rather than quietly — the price is paid knowingly, and the recent pinning work already established that this chip draws over what it crosses.

Several neighbouring rules look similar and must not be swept up: the clipped-chip floor stated in characters of the name, the chip-on-chip rule, and the no-sideways-displacement rule are each answering a different question.

The current code must be read from a FRESH clone — the primary's copy of the frontend is stale and predates the pinning rewrite this builds on.

It edits the same layout module as the halo work, so the two cannot run at the same time.

title: Epic Focus Neighbour Room
notes:
Focusing a large epic fills the panel with one band and leaves the reader no way to tell where in the plan they landed. The focus reserves a single symmetric constant on all four sides, and nothing in it knows that a neighbouring band needs a specific amount of screen height before it can show its own name — so the reservation is a number rather than an answer.

The trade is explicit and is the one being asked for: a large epic will be fitted slightly smaller so that orientation survives. The focus ceiling already makes the same trade in the other direction for tiny epics.

Three things in that function look like slack and are not: the pad is in SCREEN px so the whitespace holds at every scale, the max-of-half guard exists to remove a discontinuity where one pixel of growth changed the fit by nearly two orders of magnitude, and the scale clamp is not a duplicate of the zoom behaviour's extent — the transform is applied verbatim and only the NEXT gesture re-clamps, so removing it produces a view that looks right until the first scroll.

Reserved space is necessary and not sufficient: whether a neighbour's chip renders at that scale is decided by the sizing work immediately before this in the plan, which is why the two are sequenced rather than run together.

title: Plan Header Standard
notes:
An audit of the plan header against the two shipped visualizers, filed as the deliverable owed by the viewport work rather than as a change in itself.

Its central finding was that there is no single standard — the canonical header hides display settings behind a gear while both canvases put them on the row — and it concluded the two disagreed and one had to win. The user ruled otherwise: they are the right answers to two different questions, because a canvas is manipulated continuously while card and table views set preferences once. Nothing converges; the plan header simply adopts the canvas standard it already half-follows.

That ruling is recorded in the requirement and it unblocks the rest, which was explicitly sequenced behind it. What remains is a list of concrete deviations, each with its own reason and its own fix.

title: Requirement Link Zoom
notes:
Following a requirement's 'view on plan' link lands so far out that the thing you asked to see is a dot. The zoom is not misbehaving — the TARGET is wrong: the link focuses the requirement's EPIC, and fitting a whole epic to the viewport is by definition a zoomed-out view on a large one.

So the fix retargets rather than retunes, and it uses machinery that already exists: a parameter that names one row, with the same validation and the same transient-override behaviour the epic parameter already has. Inventing a third landing mode would be the expensive way to reach the same place.

The original description stops mid-sentence where the detail was going to be. The two instructions it did state are enough to build from, and the requirement now says which parts were written at orchestration rather than dictated — including what to do when a requirement has no step at all, which is the one case the epic fit is genuinely right for.

It edits the same detail component as the header standard, so the two cannot run at the same time.

title: Statusline Pause Word
notes:
A paused orchestration reads exactly like a live one on the status line. This renders the word; the engine change immediately before it publishes the fact, which is why the two are sequenced.

SEATED run=manual DELIBERATELY, and it is the one step here no swarm session may take. The file is carried by the user-config repo over $HOME, and a worker's write isolation refuses that path outright — a session launched against this would provision a worktree and then be blocked. The Primary executes it and deploys it through its own closeout path.

That is also why its coordination type was left as it was rather than raised: the autonomy default assumes a worker, and there is no worker here to be autonomous.

The consumer must not derive pause state itself. It runs on every render, so it reads a field from a file it already parses — and an older record with no such field renders exactly as today, because absence is not the same as paused.

title: Resync Terminal Scoping
notes: Resync is the post-/clear re-attach command for ONE terminal, so its no-argument default must never hand a second Claude session another terminal's orchestrator to Monitor and act on — measured 2026-08-02, two engines on one Mac, and the only reason no launch was doubled is that the foreign action list happened to be empty. The discriminator is terminal_pid, which survives /clear; the session id does not and would discard the very scope being reconnected. Adjacent surface: the orchestration status report work also renders engine state, so expect overlap in the render path even though the defect is in the scope filter.

title: Wall-Clock Budget Eradication
notes: An orchestrator must not stop watching a plan because a timer said so - measured 2026-08-02, an epic-scoped engine stopped itself at six hours with two sessions still running and one of them three hours from finishing, and only a manually armed watch kept the plan moving. Six hours was never argued for: the constant carries no rationale while both its neighbours do, and no decision record exists anywhere. Hazards for the implementing session: deadman is a bounded OBSERVER and keeps its budget but must stop sharing the engine constant, and pipeline-watch.sh single-gate max-polls is deliberately preserved - deleting it would remove a mechanism this work protects.

title: Aggregator Message Eradication
notes: The requirement view's aggregator card must carry no prose at all — the user reads that card constantly and wants controls, not sentences. The hazard is a narrower reading than the ask: an earlier attempt on this exact surface closed while the card still showed text, so acceptance is what the user SEES on the rendered card in every chip state, not what the diff removed. Removing text must not disturb any filtering the card performs.

title: Status Report Slim-Down
notes: The shared status report grew to answer every question anyone might ask, and the cost lands on the person reading it: the summary they wanted is buried under a plan-wide dump they have to summarise themselves, and work outside their scope is rendered under headings they read as theirs. This narrows it to one job — the minimum data behind an executive summary — and to one scope. The hazard is losing a fact rather than a section: the wide views must stay reachable on request, and the accompanying skills must be rewritten to consume the new shape rather than given a flag nobody passes.

title: Auth Description Drift
notes: Three memory documents were still describing the retired Hosted-UI + PKCE login as the current one, months after the code moved to custom screens over USER_SRP_AUTH. HAZARD: the redirect code was kept rather than removed, so the honest wording is that no routed path performs it — not that it does not exist. An earlier correction pass fixed the AWS-owned surfaces and deliberately left these to their owners.

title: Polish Pattern Rationale
notes: The Polish Pattern entry's rationale defends a property that the binding instruction text quoted in the same entry now reverses — an entry that argues against itself. HAZARD: the earlier reasoning is history worth preserving in the past tense, not an error to delete; the entry has to record what was decided, what reversed it and why.

title: Documents Registry Polish
notes: A polish pass over the documents registry surface, which grew five distinct commit models on one card with nothing telling a user which one a given control uses. HAZARD: the ask about verifying a registered location is the kind that grows a backend, so the requirement fixes that boundary rather than leaving it to judgement.

title: Agentic Patterns Home
notes: Settles where the shared patterns rulebook lives: whether it is the home for the cross-agent write-up, the shared rulebook itself, or retired. HAZARD: removal was judged expensive when this was filed, because the file was already referenced widely across the agent rows. The deliverable IS a decision about intent rather than a specification to execute, so the work stops for a human at the point the decision has to be made — which is a property of the work, not of when it may begin. It follows the rationale correction because both touch the same document, and deciding its home after its content is correct avoids deciding twice.

title: Shell Suite Flake Repair
notes: The pipeline shell suites fail a different, moving set of assertions whenever the machine is busy and pass clean when it is idle, which makes every green run unfalsifiable: a real regression is indistinguishable from load. Timing assumptions in the harness are the suspect, not the code under test.

title: Next-Up Halo At L2
notes: The next-up mark is measurably sub-pixel at the bottom of its middle zoom band and halves across the band boundary, so the one thing the plan is meant to point at is the hardest thing on it to see. An earlier pass was explicitly forbidden from touching this band; this is the half it left behind, with the measurements taken.

title: Mode Toggle Accessible Name
notes: The plan page mode switcher announces two unnamed buttons where a sighted reader sees Table and Plan — the tooltip names the icon and the icon is then hidden from the accessibility tree, so the button computes an empty name. The convergence pass that named every other control on that row was scoped out of this one.

title: Pipelines Page Viewer Header
notes: The plan LIST page hand-rolls a header the shared viewer component exists to provide, and it drifts from the card/table standard its siblings follow. That component was extracted at the moment a third hand-rolled copy appeared; this is the fourth.

title: Engine Drain Persistence
notes: A drained engine exits, so topping the plan up between waves costs a full restart with its report, its dry run and an approval gate re-authorising a grant nobody wanted re-litigated. It edits the same run-loop exit paths as the removal of the engine wall-clock bound, so the two cannot be authored at the same time.

title: Display-Only Violation Scoping
notes: Two display-order invariants are reported to every orchestrator, including ones with no way to act on them, while the five that genuinely corrupt any derivation are correctly global. Noise on the channel that carries the consequences trains the reader to skim it. Same engine module as the other run-loop work in flight, so it is authored after it rather than beside it.

title: Stall Check Primary Awareness
notes: The stall check reads only worker sessions, so work the plan coordinator performs itself is reported as stalled and the remedy it recommends would destroy that work. The fix spans the engine and the shared status report, both of which have other authoring in flight, so it follows them.

title: Plan Visualizer Polish #3
notes: One coordinated pass over the plan visualizer: the paused state reading as paused at a glance rather than through one small mark, the epic name becoming a progressive-disclosure control that zooms to what launches next, and a next-up mark that still reads below the scale where a ring cannot carry a visible stroke. They sit together because they rework the same surface and a POLISH pass is where that look-and-feel judgement is made WITH the user — the pattern prepares the deep link, subsumes the owning agent, brings up a dev server on it and then stops to discuss. That coordination is the deliverable, which is why a person starts this rather than an engine. HAZARD, accepted deliberately: these launch as concurrent sessions editing the same component, trading merge cost for one coherent visual result instead of three passes that each re-open the last.

title: Step-Note Prose Cleanup
notes: Prose that restates what a query already answers has no update path and goes stale silently, and a standing lint finding nobody acts on wears the check out. The Primary AI executes this one: step notes are a pipeline mutation, and the tool replaces rather than appends, so two writers on one plan is a violation.

title: MapsPage Toggle Accessible Name
notes: Two icon-only chart-type toggles carry no accessible name at all — a different root cause from the tooltip-inside-icon shape an earlier sweep fixed, and that sweep never looked for this shape. The group is conditionally disabled, which is exactly where a tooltip-injected label is silently lost, so the name has to be explicit.

title: Preliminaries
notes: The origin of the mapping aggregator work: everything that must exist before the card itself can be built or reviewed. Gives the mapping domain a named owner, on the same footing as every other domain, with custody of its charter and its groomed documents; and puts real mapping data in the dev database so a human can review the card without reaching into production. Both are prerequisites of the build rather than parts of it, which is why they sit at the head of the epic.

title: Condensation Advisory Removal
notes: An advisory on the plan table proposes merging steps that already launch as one command, so the merge buys nothing and costs the per-requirement titles, notes and completion signals it would collapse. It also cannot check the one condition that would make such a merge safe — whether the work can run concurrently — because that is file contention the plan data cannot see. Asking a reader for a judgement on no evidence, for a benefit already delivered, is the defect. The structure it flags is correct and stays as it is.

title: Scoped Report Violation Filtering
notes: A scoped report must cover its target scope and nothing else, because two terminals orchestrating two epics of one plan is the supported configuration and showing each of them the other rows is how a double launch starts. Display-order complaints about another tenant slice are noise on a channel that exists to be trusted; the invariants that say the shared graph is broken stay unfiltered. Gated because it must consume the invariant split the engine work introduces rather than writing a second copy that can drift.

title: Violation Dedupe Window
notes: The engine stores nothing and re-derives from the plan every cycle; one dedupe collection has no way out, so a plan that breaks the same way twice is announced once and then silently forever. A long idle window is a long time to be quiet about that. The fix is a window pruned against what the read CONTAINED rather than what was emitted, so a complaint withheld for being another scope concern stays withheld instead of returning every cycle. Gated because it edits the same suppression path the engine work is rewriting.

title: Hosted-UI Dead Code Removal
notes: The Hosted-UI login redirect stopped being reachable at the March migration to custom screens, but its components, its PKCE helper and half of authService are still shipped and still described in the memory documents. Deleting them ends the drift at its source rather than correcting the description of it a third time. The hazard is the forgot-password link on the custom login screen: it is the one Hosted-UI path a user can still click, so the callback it lands on and the AWS client configuration behind it are out of bounds for this pass.

title: Instruction Negativity Audit
notes: An instruction phrased as a prohibition tells a session what not to do without carrying the behaviour that replaces it, so it only helps a reader who has already made the mistake. This asks whether the same outcome survives being moved into the owning agent's own documentation as positive guidance. The deliverable is the classification and the recommendation; the instructions all work as they stand, so nothing is rewritten on the strength of this alone.

title: Gateway Doc Auth Flow Correction
notes: Two Data-Architect documents still name the browser's token by the flow it stopped using in March. The substantive point they are making -- two clients reaching one gateway with tokens obtained two different ways -- is correct and has to survive the correction rather than be flattened by it. Its account of which Hosted-UI code still exists is only writable once the deletion pass has settled what survives, which is why it is written second.

title: Nav Nesting, Starts Delete and Requirements Polish
notes: Three independent backlog items with disjoint file sets — the navbar config and its sidebar renderer, the swarm-starts service and its listing page, and a polish review that writes no code — seated together because they are safe to run at the same instant. HAZARD, measured 2026-08-03: the navbar carried only two levels, so moving Machines under Requirements has to INTRODUCE the nesting affordance rather than reposition a row. That finding was written into the requirement itself.

title: Requirement Editor Category Line
notes: A layout move inside the requirement editor. HAZARD: two established behaviours share this region — description autofocus once the category goes from unset to set, and a new-mode block held in layout but invisible so the fields below it do not shift. It edits the same component as the autonomy-gate work, which began first on 2026-08-03, so this rebases on that rather than racing it — two sessions in one file at the same instant is a merge conflict by construction.

title: Closeout Terminal-Write Verification
notes: Hardens the one swarm lifecycle transition that was never echo-verified — the terminal session write — and refuses the cleanup that makes a miss unrecoverable. Its own launch unit because another backlog item plans a further gate at the same closeout decision point, and both would edit the same region of the closeout command.

title: Agent Registry Closeout Plan
notes: A reflection review and a plan for tracking agents through session close, to be discussed rather than built — the plan IS the deliverable, which is why this stops for the user rather than running unattended. Gated so the plan is written against a closeout whose failure handling has already been settled, rather than against one being restructured underneath it.

title: Link Rollback Collision Guard
notes: A rollback that undoes a failed INSERT by deleting unconditionally destroys the row it collided with -- a link somebody else already owned, removed with no report to either party. That is silent data loss on a write path, and the user is told only that their own edit was rejected. The hazard is that the fix turns on telling two duplicate-key errors apart: a collision with an existing link proves the row pre-dated the step and must survive, while a second ownership claim genuinely never landed. Suppressing the cleanup for the wrong one leaves an orphan behind, so the classification has to be made deliberately rather than fall out by accident.

title: Agent Infra Leverage
notes:
The Primary AI and swarm workers adopt the agent infrastructure, rather than each carrying its own ad-hoc context assembly. The final step of the harness work: everything before it builds the infrastructure, this one makes the two main consumers actually use it.

Ordering hazard, recorded 2026-08-04: at the user's direction this step was made independent of every other epic, so it may start before the broader harness groundwork it was previously sequenced after. It must not assume that groundwork already exists.

title: Shared Telemetry Harness
notes:
One telemetry record definition and one run harness, shared by two domains that measure the same kind of thing — a Claude run — with entirely separate machinery.

Surveyed 2026-08-01. Swarm sessions carry phase accumulators, wall-clock and token totals, plus a free-text blob scraped out of three ad-hoc stdout conventions. Agent telemetry carries a ten-way context-composition breakdown written by five one-off scripts.

The shared part is the MEASUREMENT ENVELOPE, not the container. Model, effort, machine, timestamp, wall clock and tokens are defined twice and already disagree — wall clock is seconds on one side and milliseconds on the other, and the token concepts do not overlap at all. Neither side captures the input prompt, nor the full four-way token usage.

The domain decompositions stay domain-specific: phase accumulators are a session concept, context breakdown is an agent concept, and flattening them into one table would make both worse.

Scoped as a decision taken with the user rather than an invention made inside an implementation, because the durable signal itself is the question. Three options are costed; a staged adoption is explicitly allowed.

Ordering hazard, recorded 2026-08-04: at the user's direction this step was made independent of every other epic, so it may start before the broader harness groundwork it was previously sequenced after. It must not assume that groundwork already exists.

title: Stage 1 - First Principles Plan
notes: Settle what the rebuild is before anyone builds it: the containment chain, the concepts that remain, the concepts that go, and what each removal costs - measured rather than asserted. Its output is a reviewable object, which is the point. A design decided silently inside an implementation cannot be reviewed at all.

title: Stage 2 - Data Architecture & Design Intent
notes: The shape of the data comes first because every other panel member designs against it. Containment expressed in the DDL rather than in convention, and the registration gates satisfied from the schema rather than by hand. The hazard is scope: this settles a design and applies nothing.

title: Stage 2 - Architect Panel
notes: Each architect tests the plan against the code it actually owns and authors the build work for its own domain. This is where stage-one assumptions meet the people positioned to find them wrong, and it is deliberately wide because the members are independent. The hazard is two members specifying the same thing differently, which is invisible from inside either one.

title: Stage 2 - Seat Stage 3 Requirements
notes: One designated writer puts the authored work into the plan, because concurrent writers lose updates silently and the loss leaves no error behind. Adjusting the sequence is expected here: the sequence was authored before the panel ran, and the panel is the reason it exists.

title: Stage 2 - Plan Review
notes: The gate at the end of the planning stages. Everything the panel decided, everything it could not decide, and what each unresolved question would cost - put in front of a person before any of it is built. It holds the run deliberately: a plan whose overturned assumptions nobody reviewed is a plan being executed on trust rather than on agreement.

title: 2.0 Schema & Parallel Tables
notes: Bring the new plan layer up beside the existing one so both eras can run at once. Nothing is removed and nothing reaches the live database here: containment is expressed in the DDL rather than in convention, and the ownership registries are derived from that DDL rather than hand-counted. The hazard is those registries - a security test satisfied by bumping a count is a green suite with vacuous coverage, which is worse than a red one because nobody looks again.

title: 2.0 MCP Read Surface
notes: The plan must be readable before anything can orchestrate it: one composed read for the whole plan at a fixed cost regardless of size, and the same payload narrowed to a single epic. Session attribution is re-pointed onto the same walk in the same unit of work, because one walk yielding both columns is what makes them unable to disagree. The hazard is the payload budget - withholding the convenience block before truncating rows keeps every row in the band where the older shape lost them all.

title: 1.0 to 2.0 Importer
notes: Carry the existing plan into the new shape repeatedly and without fear, because the first era stays in production while this is debugged. Copy shapes as they are; translate only what the target can express and the source cannot.

title: Derivation - Single Source of Truth
notes: Step state, ordering and launch arguments computed in exactly one place. The same rules currently exist twice in two languages, kept honest by a corpus that can detect divergence but never prevent it. A second implementation is a standing promise to drift.

title: Swarm Step Addressing
notes: Make the step something the swarm can be pointed at directly - one command, one step, the sessions its ready work needs. The resolver is extended rather than duplicated, because two resolvers with different ambiguity semantics is the drift this rebuild exists to remove and it would arrive with the first divergent edit. The hazard is a resolver that guesses: no input may silently resolve to work nobody named, because what follows a resolution is clones, branches, draft PRs and terminals.

title: Orchestration Engine - Step as Launch Unit
notes: One step, all of its ready work, one announcement, any width - so launch overhead stops being paid once per requirement - together with the parallel command family that drives it, which comes up beside the older one rather than in place of it. One predicate answers "should I announce this?", replacing two mechanisms that answered it differently. The concurrency ceiling is absent from this engine in every form, which is a deletion rather than a move, and re-introducing it under a new name is a regression.

title: Visualizer 2.0 - Batch Leaves the Drawing
notes: The concept that assembled several steps into one announcement leaves the surface, because the step is the announcement now. The view is not otherwise redesigned and the obvious hazard is scope creep dressed as polish. The quieter one is that the launch payload this concept carried must land on the row that replaces it - deleting it from the only surface that shows it would be a loss rather than a cleanup, and the oldest invariant on this surface must keep running over its fuzz corpus after the machinery beside it goes.

title: Reservations Across Both Eras
notes: The reservation table is the one piece of the parallel era that can stop the older one working, and the older one is the plan that builds this. Sharing is right and re-pointing is wrong: a foreign key is a static declaration rather than an alternation, and two independent id sequences make a numerically valid wrong answer possible - which for a mutual-exclusion device is worse than failing outright. The hazard is blurring a live claim reclaimed on staleness with a user intention that must never be.

title: Visualizer 2.0 - Test Plan & Tests
notes: The visualizer gets testing of its own rather than a testing clause inside its implementation, because rendering defects are the ones that survive unit tests and reach the user.

title: The 2.0 Document & Doctrine
notes: One document that reads as though the system always was this way, with every generation-to-generation difference confined to a single appendix - and the two mechanisms that make the one-fact-in-one-place rule bind rather than merely be stated. The hazard is history leaking back one sentence at a time, which is why the appendix boundary is a check and not a convention.

title: Performance - Telemetry & Optimization Report
notes: Measure what each command costs in tokens and wall clock, optimise against the measurement, and report both numbers. Held for review on purpose - a performance claim nobody reads is a performance claim nobody checked.

title: Feature Eradication - Drop the Schema
notes: The last removal before the older layer itself goes: the table, the junction and the column every other surface has already stopped reading. Ordering is the whole of the safety here, and every precondition is verified by running something rather than by reading a diff. The hazard is a row count assumed to be zero - if links still exist this stops being a drop and becomes a migration, and the mapping it would destroy cannot be recovered afterwards.

title: 1.0 Eradication
notes: Retire the older layer once the newer one has been watched doing its job and the cost of running it is known. Last on purpose: an eradication that precedes its evidence is a rollback waiting to happen.

title: 2.0 Production Schema
notes: New tables on the live database is the one place in this epic where a person genuinely has to say yes, so it is its own unit of work rather than a clause inside the DDL authoring. The migration already exists and has already been verified against the development database; what happens here is the apply and the proof that the older era's tables were not disturbed. The hazard is that the era being rebuilt is also the era running this plan - an apply that damages it stops the programme that authorized it.

title: 2.0 Gateway Routes
notes: Five tables per stage cost ten console-built resources, and until they exist the tables are unreachable by any reader, writer, test or importer. It sits where it does because the acceptance is a successful read on every one of the ten, and half of them address the production database. The hazard is improvising the AWS calls the route script already makes: there is no new cost here and no policy change, and both must be verified against a before-image rather than asserted.

title: The Test-Case Junction in Production
notes: The sixth table of this programme, and the one every other piece of work assumed somebody else would apply. Live DDL is a user gate for the same reason the plan-layer apply is. The hazard is a stale row count: the figure that decides whether the later drop destroys live links was recorded as zero in two places and re-measured as twenty-eight, so it is re-taken here rather than quoted.

title: 2.0 Plan-Layer Tools and Derivation
notes: The mutation surface and the derivation module, both written against the composed read and neither against the other. Every mutation returns the state it changed, read back from the database, so a caller can verify rather than hope; the derivation loses the label walk outright, because containment answers with a column what the older shape reconstructed by tally. The hazard is a second live copy - neither may reach into the older modules, which are still running the plan that builds this one.

title: Visualizer 2.0 - The Browser Consumes the Composed Read
notes: The panel stops assembling a model out of six dictionary reads and receives one composed payload instead, so the client-side derivation is deleted rather than re-pointed. It is placed where it is because the drawing work is scoped to the drawing precisely on the assumption that the fetch and the model are already gone. The hazard is a withheld or truncated derived block rendering as a smaller plan: a browser draws silently, where an engine at least writes a line nobody can miss.

title: Visualizer 2.0 - Epic Containment in the Render
notes: Bands keyed on a column rather than on a tally, and band order taken from the author's stored epic sequence rather than derived from start dates, so the canvas and the table stop being one plan drawn two ways. It is kept apart from the other drawing work because it rewrites the same layout module at its widest point, and two concurrent editors there lose each other's work with no error. The trade is stated rather than discovered: a stored sequence can place an epic whose work started earlier below one that has not begun, and the horizontal axis is what makes that the right trade.

title: Visualizer 2.0 - Polish List
notes: A list of named defects and stale mechanisms on this surface, each independently strikeable by the user: comments naming a deleted function, a permissive default, a cap on the cheaper axis, and measured tables that no longer describe the code. It is placed after the concept removals because several of its numbers are downstream of them, and before the look-and-feel pass, because a pass taken against stale measurements is a pass taken against the wrong numbers.

title: Swarm Step-Addressed Execution
notes: A resolved step expands into one session per requirement, launched together, with two de-duplication guards for two different situations and no new column anywhere. It is sequenced behind the addressing and admission work because all three edit the same launch skill. The hazard is a partially launched unit, which the plan cannot represent: the step reads as underway off the items that did start, while part of its work has not begun.

title: Feature Eradication - MCP, Scripts, Frontend and the Instruction Rows
notes: The intermediate tier leaves everything that reached through it, in four areas that share a deadline and almost no files. One of those areas is not in the file tree at all: two instruction rows do not merely mention the tier, they teach it, and an agent booting after the drop would be told to call a tool that no longer exists, failing at run time with nothing tying the failure back. The hazard everywhere else is a test suite that goes green because its subject vanished, which is not evidence.

title: The Verification Register and the Coverage Gate
notes: The register that states what this rebuild must do is reconciled against the design records that did not exist when it was written, and the gate that asserts coverage is wired into the acceptance of the work it governs. It comes first because that wiring REWRITES the specification of work that has not started, and a session already reading its spec will never see the edit. The hazard is the reverse of the usual one: arriving late does not fail loudly, it silently reduces a gate to decoration.

title: Visualizer 2.0 - Feature Leaves the Drawing
notes: The label path and the second grouping tier leave the surface, and the control that pointed at the page listing an epic's work gets a target that still exists. It is kept apart from the other concept removal because the two rewrite the same row-rendering function, and two branches editing one function merge into something neither session ran. The hazard is silence: a link to a removed route builds cleanly and fails only when a reader clicks it.

title: Swarm Admission and the Concurrency Ceiling
notes: How much may run at once stops being a plan-side arithmetic and becomes one constant in the launch path, enforced at admission against a live count of this machine's sessions, all-or-nothing, with nobody ever asked. It is sequenced rather than shared because it edits the same launch skill as the addressing work. Four attempts were spent learning that a per-run knob cannot be made safe, so the hazard is any route back to one: a flag, a record field, a config file, an environment variable, or a prompt.

title: Per-Machine Concurrency Ceiling (machines.max_live_sessions)
notes: Stage-2 gate ruling: the ceiling becomes per-machine data before the admission requirement consumes it. Shares the DarwinSQL parity artifacts (schema.sql, recreate, test_data_types) with the reservations migration, so the two cannot run concurrently — the edge carries that.

notes: The user's 2026-08-07 launch-args status rule lands before stage 3 rewrites the surfaces it names. Edits swarm-start.md, which the swarm chain serializes on — the edges carry that.

notes: Stage-2 gate C-12: edits the visualizer files the serialized 2.0 drawing chain rewrites, so it runs after that chain's tests, one at a time — the chain edges carry that.

notes: Stage-2 gate C-12: edits the visualizer files the serialized 2.0 drawing chain rewrites, so it runs after that chain's tests, one at a time — the chain edges carry that.

notes: HELD 2026-08-10. Its requirement caused a production outage in the mirror image of req #3381 and is halted at authoring pending a re-scope; this step must not auto-launch until the user re-approves it. Set back to auto in the same act that re-approves the requirement.

notes: Split from the read-service step by the gate review pass (X1): both requirements edit darwin-mcp/services/requirements.py, and the attribution migration joins the schema.sql cohort — the edges carry both facts.

title: Orchestrated-Requirements Visibility Toggle
notes: The view-wide control that hides requirements a plan already sequences is the one surface that tells a reader which work is spoken for. While it reports wrongly, the card views cannot be trusted to answer that question at all.

title: Legacy Phase-Bucket Row in darwin_dev
notes: A data condition, not a code defect: it fails for every session that runs the DarwinSQL suite until the row is resolved, so it reads as this session's breakage to whoever hits it.

title: Delete Guard Below the Application Layer
notes: The guard exists in two places the browser never reaches. Putting it where the rows live is what makes it true regardless of which client issues the delete.

title: Restart Resumes the Conversation
notes: A restart that reconstructs from artifacts recovers what was written down and loses what was reasoned. Resuming the transcript is the difference between continuing and starting again.

title: Three Red Shell Suites
notes: Suites that are red before a change begins cost every later session the work of proving the failure is not theirs, and eventually get read past entirely.

title: Epic Composability
notes: A question to settle with the user before anything is built, so it is a conversation the plan makes room for rather than one a session opens unattended and waits out.

title: Serial Mode Made Visible
notes: The mode changes which work the plan will start, and a reader looking at the running system cannot currently see that it is in force or which scope holds the rest. A held step reports a cause that is not its own.

title: Engine Lifetime Measured, Not Assumed
notes: The two possible answers give opposite operator advice, and one of them leaves an orchestrator running with nobody watching it and nothing that would say so.

title: Blast Radius of the Execution-Mode Column
notes: A column that exists in the database and in the migration but not in every artifact that describes the database is invisible to whichever surface was missed, and the gap reports as a failure belonging to whoever next runs the suite.

title: Instructions Table Rendering
notes: A table whose first columns are unreadable cannot be scanned, which is the only thing a table is for. Bounding what the long field shows keeps the row legible and leaves the full text where there is room to read it.

title: Epic Review With the User
notes: Nothing downstream is worth building until somebody who can say what this epic is FOR has read what it became. The decomposition was written in one pass by the session that closed the work defining it, and a plan nobody argued with is a plan whose mistakes are found at the end. This sits in front of the epic so that reading it is unavoidable rather than optional.

title: Priority Polish
notes: Small surface defects the user hits often enough to name. One of them has already been filed twice, which is the argument for fixing the pattern rather than the instance.

title: Priority Polish #2
notes: The second round of user-selected polish, opened while the first round is still in flight. It is a separate launch unit rather than an addition to the round before it so that work arriving after that round started is not held behind it.

title: Pipeline 2.0 - Orchestrator Stability
notes: Three separate ways an automated run stops without saying so: a prompt nobody is there to answer, an approval whose necessity depends on how the work was filed, and an engine whose reporting drowns its own signal. Grouped because the operator experiences them as one thing - the run looked healthy and was not moving.

title: Survey and Profile
notes: Two surveys that share no file. One enumerates the rule surface a swarm session receives and writes a new inventory document; the other settles what an orchestrator session may and may not do, inside the orchestration documents that already own that area. Neither is an input to the other, so running them together buys the whole of the second phase an earlier start.

title: Boot Contract, Provisioning and Doctrine
notes: Design-only work beside two builds with disjoint targets: the provisioning change owns the session scripts, the manifest schema and the write-isolation guard, while the doctrine work owns the orchestration documents and the rulebook's plan-authority section. The doctrine work is placed here deliberately — it is one of three pieces of work in this epic that edit the workspace rulebook, and this is the only point at which it can hold that file alone.

title: Build the Session Definition Mechanism
notes: The composition service and both terminal launch backends on one side; the pipeline skills, the reservation and the primary-only guards on the other. Disjoint file sets, so they run at once. The composition work carries the coordination procedures with it because both edit the same files — that is why it is one requirement rather than two.

title: Prove the Harness and Consume It
notes: The mechanism gets its suite and its first hard consumer in the same round. The consumer is defined largely by exclusions, which is what a definition format is most likely to be unable to express; finding that while the suite is being written is the point, and a suite alone would not find it. One writes test files, the other writes registry rows.

title: Retire the Prose, Test the Orchestrator
notes: Deletion from the prose files, on the evidence the suite produced, beside the orchestrator's own end-to-end coverage. The deletion owns the rulebook and the launch scripts; the coverage owns test files. The before-and-after measurement travels with the deletion because only the session that deletes can take the after-figure on the same method.

title: Design the Primary Boot, Show the Roster
notes: Design work that builds nothing, beside the registry pages. The pages do not wait on the Primary booting from a definition: their own acceptance requires rendering honestly what is still file-resident, so they can tell the truth about the Primary before it moves and keep telling it afterwards.

title: The Primary Boots From Its Definition
notes: Alone because it is squeezed from both sides: it edits the composition surface the registry pages render, and it owns the boot path the Primary's suite asserts against. Either pairing would put two sessions in one file set.

title: Prove the Primary and Its Fallback
notes: Alone because its coverage reaches back over both the registry pages and the boot path, and a suite cannot assert against work being written beneath it. The fallback announcement is part of the assertion: a silent correct fallback is indistinguishable from a normal boot.

title: Retire the Monolith
notes: The rulebook stops being the authority and becomes the template. Alone because it is the third piece of work in this epic to edit that file and the last to do so, and because it may only run on evidence the suites have already produced.

title: Close the Cost Model
notes: The capstone. It answers whether this epic's opening premise held — that a session assembling its own context is expensive and unmeasurable — including the case where the honest answer is that it did not. Every earlier piece of work is implied through the gate it carries.

title: Pipeline 2.0 Production Breakage - Re-align and Re-land #3381
notes: Front of the line. 2.0 took production down by re-pointing a live 1.0 surface at 2.0 data; the standing terms are that 1.0 stays unaltered while 2.0 stands up beside it. This step exists so the browser-side 2.0 consumption comes back in a form that cannot repeat that, and so a green build alone can no longer ship a page whose data source moved.

title: Visualizer Polish #1
notes: Edits the same visualizer files as the preceding polish work, so it cannot run concurrently with them.
